before.heading: Research
before.body:
At the end of the first paragraph, we get our only sentence about "magnetite grains".

These grains are within magma and react to the Earth's magnetic field, pointing towards whichever side is positively charged, presumably.

When magma cools, if the magnetite grain is pointing towards the North Pole, then the north-leaning grain will forever lean that way.

If the magnetic field is such that the South Pole has the positive charge, then when magma cools, the magnetite grains in it will point toward the South Pole forever.

Since we know that the magnetic field has reversed at various times throughout history (and since we presume there has been lava / magma at all times throughout history), we could infer that different magnetite grains will be pointing in different directions.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body: Find something that plays off our understanding that when magma cools, the magnetite's leaning direction gets locked in like a photograph of where the Earth's magnetic field was at the time.

after.heading: Research
after.body: In molten magma, magnetite grains align with Earths magnetic field. Cooling locks in that alignment, recording the fields polarity then. Paragraph 3 directly states that the youngest rocks have normal polarity, meaning alignment with the present field. Keep magnetic polarity distinct from positive and negative electrical charge.

after.heading: Anticipate

corrections.before:
The youngest basalt means the magma that has most recently cooled.

If there's a volcanic eruption in Hawaii right now, then the magma that explodes out will eventually cool into basalt, and the magnetite grain will show a snapshot of the earth's current polarity.

The only way for this answer to not be true would be if the Earth's magnetic field had switched polarity since the most recent eruption of magma. But the magnetic field has reversed "at various times" over the course of Earth's 4 billion year history, suggesting that the magnetic field switches every few million years.

In our lifetime, the magnetic field has never switched. Thus, any magma that has cooled in our lifetime will form basalt whose magnetite grains are pointing at the current polarity of the magnetic field.
corrections.after: Paragraph 3 explicitly says the youngest rocks all have normal polarity. Paragraph 1 defines normal polarity as the same polarity as Earths present magnetic field. Those two statements directly support the answer without estimating reversal frequency or invoking modern eruptions.

corrections.before:

There's nothing special about the peak of the mid-ocean ridge connected to being out of whack. To the contrary, since that's where the new magma spew out of, that has the youngest basalt and thus it should usually have cooled in alignment with the current polarity of the Earth's magnetic field. Thus, if you're near the peak of the mid-ocean ridge, you're dealing with modern basalt, it's aligned, so it won't distort.
corrections.after: The youngest rocks near the ridge have normal polarity, but the passage does not establish where compass distortion is most likely or that normal-polarity basalt cannot distort a reading. Variable reversal intervals instead predict unequal stripe widths.

corrections.before:
Almost none of us would be attracted to this answer on the first pass. It seems to just be signing off the on the truth of a "Premise".

One of the strongest pieces of evidence for ocean-floor spreading was the "remarkable correlation" between the ages of the earth's magnetic reversals and the striping pattern found near the mid-ocean ridge.

We were told that the ages of the earth's magnetic reversals "had been assigned by measuring the magnetic orientation of continental volcanic rocks, whose ages we had already determined".

In other words, we had already decided how old a bunch of rocks were near a volcano on land, and those rocks have the compass needle thing that tells us whether the Earth was in normal polarity (positive North Pole / negative South Pole) or reversed polarity.

So if they had a 300 million year old volcanic rock with reversed polarity and a 250 million year old volcanic rock with normal polarity, they would decide that "the earth's polarity switched between 250-300 million years ago".

All this answer is saying is that cross-referenced that timeline we built with some other means to verify that our timeline of magnetic reversals was correct.

By verifying our timeline, we make it a more trustworthy metric of when polarity changed, and so the "remarkable correlation" between mid-ocean stripes and the polarity timeline feels even more *real* than before.

But this answer does nothing new. None of us were worried that the polarity timeline derived from the volcanic rocks was messed up. We had never been told it was definitely right, and now this answer is telling us it's definitely right.

It's a very, very bizarre answer. It's has very little strengthening effect, but it's more than nothing, and more than every other answer, so that makes it the winner.
corrections.after: The correlation depends on the assigned dates of magnetic reversals. Independent verification of those dates makes the correlation more trustworthy and therefore strengthens its support for spreading. Strengthening can reinforce the reliability of a premise; it need not supply a wholly new kind of evidence or settle the theory beyond doubt.

corrections.before:
There are only two polarities, normal or inverted (positive charge on the North pole or on the South pole).

The earth's magnetic field has oscillated back and forth between normal and reversed polarity many times through Earth's history. If we're currently on version 100 of earth's magnetic field, then we have same polarity as version 98, 96, 94, etc.

Any rock that was formed during version 98, 96, 94, etc., would exhibit present-day magnetic polarity, even though it wasn't formed during version 100.

If we think about the striping pattern on the ocean floor ... every 2nd stripe will have rocks that match present-day polarity.
corrections.after: Polarity has reversed more than once, and the ocean floor alternates between stripes with normal and reversed polarity. An older stripe can therefore match the present field as well. Matching current polarity does not uniquely identify formation after the latest reversal; the answer confuses a recurring condition with a unique timestamp.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
In general, a conspiracy theory involves the idea of an apparent truth which belies a very different (often darker) truth.

There are conspiracy theories about JFK's assassination. The apparent truth is that Lee Harvey Oswald was a lone gunman who did the deed. The conspiracy theory is that the FBI was behind the whole thing.

The apparent truth about covid vaccines is that they are an emergency response to a global health crisis. The conspiracy theory is that they are a tool Bill Gates is using to implant 5G chips into people.

So when it comes to genes, what's the apparent truth and what's the deeper, more sinister truth?

The apparent, unsurprising truth is that "You care about your children because you love them".

The conspiracy theory is that "you care about your children because your genes care only about replication and your children are the replicants of your genes, so the genes **make** you care about your children in order to protect the precious copies of the genes inside your kids".

before.heading: Goal
before.body: So what part of Passage A matches up with "your genes make you care about your kids in order to safeguard the copies of those genes that exist inside your kids"?

after.heading: Anticipate
after.body: B defines the comparison directly: a behavior is explained through an interest that its agent does not acknowledge or know about. Its example contrasts an ordinary concern for a child with genes promoting their own replication. Look for A assigning that underlying genetic function to apparently unselfish behavior, without treating genes as literally plotting agents.

before.heading: Anticipate

The author of B presents an argument similar to that of psg A in the first paragraph of psg B.

In the second paragraph, the author of B explains how this argument sounds persuasive on the face of it. She ends the paragraph asking, "is the conclusion they draw from this evidence right? Maybe yes, maybe no."

So the "assumption" we're looking for should be something that comes from the third paragraph of passage B. Assumptions are the opposite of Objections, so if we find an objection we can always flip that into an assumption.

Passage B's objection is that "even though you *could* explain altruism or a mom's concern for her kid in terms of evolutionary outcomes, you could also explain it in terms of the unsurprising idea that moms love their kids."

Since passage B's objection to the type of argument made in passage A is that "other explanations may exist", she would probably say that the EP's are assuming that "you can ****only**** explain behavior in evolutionary terms".

corrections.before:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The 1980s rise of Latina autobiography — innovative collections by Moraga, Levins Morales/Morales, and Anzaldúa — and how these writers experimented with the genre.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author celebrates how Latina autobiographers pushed past traditional generic boundaries to express the complexities of their identities.

**Main Point**

Latina autobiographers of the 1980s revolutionized the genre, redrawing its boundaries to make it more amenable to expressing the complexity of their multiple cultural identities. They mixed languages, mixed genres, and even mixed authorial voices.

**P1: The 1980s flourishing**

The 1980s saw a proliferation of poetry, short stories, and novels by U.S. Latinas, plus the autobiography genre coming into prominence with three notable collections: Moraga's *Loving in the War Years*, Levins Morales/Morales's *Getting Home Alive*, and Anzaldúa's *Borderlands/La Frontera*.

**P2: The collections' shared innovations**

They mix English and Spanish (linguistic boundaries), explore intersections of ethnicity, gender, and language (multiple cultural identities), and combine essays, sketches, short stories, poems, and journal entries (generic mixing) without giving preference to any one mode.

**P3: Three concrete examples — and the most experimental, *Getting Home Alive***

Anzaldúa juxtaposes narrative and poetry. Moraga mixes genres and arranges events by political development rather than chronology — a difference critics see between women's and men's autobiographies. *Getting Home Alive* goes furthest from convention: it has two authors (mother and daughter), woven together rather than separated, with one piece sometimes commenting on the other. The ordering may seem fragmentary but is fully intentional. The mixing of structures parallels the content — multigeneric and multivocal forms expressing the complexities of identity formation.

**P4: The achievement**

Rather than forcing personal histories into existing generic parameters, these writers have revolutionized autobiography, redrawing its boundaries to better express their experiences and showing a strong determination to speak for themselves.

The 1980s saw a proliferation of poetry, short stories, and novels by U.S. Latinas, plus the autobiography genre coming into prominence with three notable collections: Moraga's *Loving in the War Years*, Levins Morales/Morales's *Getting Home Alive*, and Anzaldúa's *Borderlands/La Frontera*.

**P2: The collections' shared innovations**

They mix English and Spanish (linguistic boundaries), explore intersections of ethnicity, gender, and language (multiple cultural identities), and combine essays, sketches, short stories, poems, and journal entries (generic mixing) for the most part without giving preference to any one mode.

**P3: Three concrete examples — and the most experimental, *Getting Home Alive***

Anzaldúa juxtaposes narrative and poetry. Moraga mixes genres and arranges events by political development rather than chronology — a difference critics see between women's and men's autobiographies. *Getting Home Alive* goes furthest from convention: it has two authors (mother and daughter), woven together rather than separated, with one piece sometimes commenting on the other. The ordering may seem fragmentary but is fully intentional. The mixing of structures parallels the content — multigeneric and multivocal forms expressing the complexities of identity formation.

**P4: The achievement**

Rather than forcing personal histories into existing generic parameters, these writers have revolutionized autobiography, redrawing its boundaries to better express their experiences and showing a strong determination to speak for themselves.

corrections.before:

*GHA* goes "even further" in the same direction.

In a sense, it would be an oxymoron to classify any of these three as belonging to a "type", since they are *innovative*, meaning they haven't been done before. If you're the first of your kind, you don't belong to a type. And you haven't invented a "type" until others follow a similar template.

**Topic**

The risk of losing modern information due to the fragility and rapid obsolescence of recording and storage technologies.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

Although we now create and save more information than ever, the materials and technologies we use to store this information are increasingly fragile and quickly become outdated, making it very challenging for archivists to preserve important records for the future. **P1: The Fragility of Modern Storage Media**

We learn that even though we're recording tons of information these days, we're at greater risk than ever of losing it, mainly because modern recording materials (like acidic paper, color photos, and videotapes) are way less durable than the old stuff (like clay tablets or parchment). So, archivists are stuck dealing with this paradox of more information but less reliable media.

**P2: Technology's Double-Edged Sword**

It might seem like saving everything digitally would solve this problem, but rapid changes in technology can make stored information inaccessible surprisingly quickly. For example, data saved on older computer disks can become unreadable as the software and hardware change, and even new digital tapes only last about ten years. Archivists are feeling the pressure as time runs out for both old and new media.

**P3: The Tough Choices Archivists Face**

Even if we develop storage tech that finally lasts, archivists will still have to decide what is worth saving—fast—since things are deteriorating all the time. Figuring out the value of each item is tricky, as history has already lost some great works simply because no one realized their importance at the time. The real danger now is that there is just so much stuff, stored on media that doesn't last, that archivists might not be able to sort and save what's most important before it's too late.

**Topic**

The legal reasoning behind why blackmail is (or isn't) considered a crime in different legal traditions.

**Framework**

Present Debate (two approaches to blackmail: North American law grapples with a "paradox," while Roman law frames blackmail differently)

**Main Point**

Passage A: Blackmail is paradoxical in North American law because it combines two legal actions into an illegal one, but its criminality can be justified by the misuse of third-party leverage. *(Most valuable sentences: “The heart of the problem—known as the blackmail paradox—is that two acts, each of which is legally permissible separately, become illegal when combined.”, and “Thus, blackmail is criminal because it involves the misuse of a third party for the blackmailer’s own benefit.”)*
Passage B: Roman law avoided the blackmail paradox by valuing whether actions caused harm, not just their legality, and placed the burden on the possessor of shameful information to justify disclosure, even if the information was true.

**P1A: Blackmail Paradox Introduced**

Both the U.S. and Canadian laws find blackmail odd because it criminalizes two actions (asking for money and threatening to disclose information) that are each legal on their own, raising the question: why is their combination illegal?

**P2A: Problems Without a Theory**

Because legal theory hasn't satisfactorily explained blackmail, laws are overly broad and rely on prosecutors to use discretion in enforcement.

**P3A: Author’s Solution: Third-Party Leverage**

The real issue with blackmail is its “triangular” structure—the blackmailer uses a threat of outside harm (like state prosecution or public shame) as leverage, which is why it should be criminalized.

**P1B: Roman Law’s Approach — Harm First**

In Roman law, blackmail wasn’t treated as a special crime; instead, jurists looked at whether an action, like revealing information, actually caused harm.

**P2B: Burden on the Discloser**

Roman law assumed that revealing shameful secrets would harm someone, so the person threatening or revealing the info had to prove they had a legitimate reason for doing so.

**P3B: Truth Isn’t a Blank Check**

Even if the information was true, it could only be lawfully revealed for a legitimate reason and for public benefit. Just being true wasn’t enough to make exposure legally acceptable.

corrections.before:
The idea of the blackmail paradox in US / Canadian law is that you have the right to tell someone's embarrassing secret (because of free speech) and you have the right to seek money.

But when you combine the idea of seeking money or else you'll tell someone's embarrassing secret, then it somehow becomes a crime called blackmail.

Meanwhile, in Roman law, they didn't have a special category / crime called blackmail. They didn't need to say, "Sure, you're allowed, via free speech protection, to say an embarrassing secret someone else is keeping, but if you ****charge money for it****, then it becomes an illegal thing called blackmail."

Instead, in their system they would just assess whether a given action caused harm or not. Revealing someone's embarrassing secret was assumed to be harmful to them. If revealing their secret would harm their status or reputation, then revealing their secret was unlawful (as was threatening to do so).

Your "right" to reveal someone's secret wasn't protected by free speech. It could be against the law for you to utter this secret if doing so would harm the person.

As the beginning of the 3rd paragraph of B says,
*assertion of the truth of the shameful fact being revealed was not, in itself, sufficient to constitute a legal privilege*.

Meanwhile, in US / Canadian law, you are allowed to reveal the shameful fact. If it's true, you're not guilty of slander or libel, and free speech protections grant you the right to say it.
corrections.after: A presents disclosure as independently permissible under its free-speech account, which creates the two-permissible-acts paradox. B instead says harmful disclosure is presumptively unlawful even if true, unless justified by a legitimate purpose and a public-authority interest. That removes the premise needed for the paradox. These are the passages' contrasting accounts, not a universal statement that every true disclosure is legally protected today.

corrections.before:
We only know that when it comes to free speech protection, Canadian and US law grant more freedoms, insofar as their legal systems grant the freedom to reveal a shameful but true fact about someone else, whereas Roman law does not grant this freedom.

But we wouldn't be able to comment on whether the sum total of Canadian / US common law granted more freedoms than did classical Roman law.
corrections.after: The passages contrast protection for the particular disclosures involved in blackmail. B treats harmful disclosure as presumptively unlawful, while allowing disclosure for a legitimate purpose concerning a matter public authorities have an interest in having revealed. This limited comparison does not establish which system grants more freedoms in general.

corrections.before:
Just because the "interest of public authorities of having certain info revealed" is language that is only used at the end of Passage B doesn't mean we can assume that Canadian and US law don't ever recognize the same interest.

We probably know from outside knowledge that Canadian and US law will allow judges to issue warrants or subpoenas that allow federal authorities to obtain or reveal information that's important to an investigation.

To say that North American legal systems do not in any way recognize that public authorities may sometimes have an interest in having certain information revealed would be a very extreme, unlikely claim.
corrections.after: A explicitly identifies the state's interest as leverage in the example of threatening to report a crime. B also recognizes public authorities' interest in disclosure. The proposed contrast is therefore unsupported without importing external law.

corrections.before:
In the US / CA system, it is separately legal to charge someone money for services rendered and legal to expose someone's criminal act or embarrassing private information, so we can say that blackmail is comprised of two separately legal actions.

In the Roman system, it is ****not**** legal to expose someone's embarrassing private information, so we couldn't say that blackmail is comprised of two separately legal actions.
corrections.after: In A's account, seeking money and disclosure are each separately permissible. In B, disclosure that harms status or reputation is presumptively unlawful and requires a positive justification. Thus the combination does not begin with the same two-permissible-acts premise. B does allow specified legitimate disclosures; it does not prohibit all disclosure of private information.

corrections.before:
We don't have any support for affirming that in US / CA law the blackmail laws are meant to be enforced ****precisely as written****.

And in Roman law there was no category for blackmail, so it's not even really true to say that there *were* laws pertaining to blackmail, in the direct sense. Thus it would be weird to say, "in Roman law, the laws pertaining to blackmail (which don't exist) were not meant to be enforced precisely as written."
corrections.after: A says blackmail statutes are overly broad and rely on prosecutors not to enforce them precisely as written. So the first half is unsupported. B's lack of a special blackmail category does not mean no laws applied: its broader rules against harmful disclosure made a separate category unnecessary.

corrections.before:
The first law, representing the CA / USA system, is more restrictive than the second one.

That would be the opposite of what we're looking for.

One country (ROME) requires that anyone revealing shameful info about someone else have a legitimate, publicly-endorsed reason for doing so; another country (CA / USA) has no such requirement (free speech allows you to reveal it).

B begins with a broader restriction on harmful disclosure, allowing it only for a legitimate purpose concerning a matter public authorities have an interest in having revealed. The licensing requirement in the first country therefore does not match A's role.

corrections.before:

corrections.before:

But it doesn't seem a great match. The US/CA notions of free speech are pretty much that it's unlimited (as long as you're not blackmailing someone). It's not like more free speech is allowed in US/CA because of loopholes or exceptions. It's just the default position of US/CA is that you can say what you want (in most circumstances) and the default position of Rome is that you can't say what you want if it's going to be harmful to someone else (in most circumstances).
corrections.after: A numerical comparison of exceptions does not capture the structure: one system specifically prohibits a combination while the other has a broader prohibition that already covers the conduct, subject to limited legitimate exceptions. corrections.before:
The second one is more restrictive: "by default, you can't have guns, unless you have some legitimate public purpose".

The first one is less restrictive: "by default, you can have guns, but not if you combine it with being a felon".

corrections.after: The first country specifically prohibits one combination: gun ownership by felons. The second country's broader prohibition already covers that combination, with exceptions for police and the military. Similarly, A specifically prohibits the blackmail combination, while B's broader restriction on harmful disclosure makes a separate blackmail category unnecessary. B permits disclosure only when it has a legitimate purpose and concerns a matter public authorities have an interest in having revealed.

corrections.before:
If we skip to the ending and see "a modification of the hypothesis is argued for", we don't need to read the rest.

A hypothesis is a causal explanation for something that transpired or is transpiring. This passage isn't focused on solving the causal mystery of how this soil got depleted. It is forward-looking, trying to come up with a plan to fix this problem.

So in the last paragraph, the author is definitely not saying, "I think we should somewhat modify the causal story you're telling for why X happened."
corrections.after: A hypothesis can concern a future result as well as explain a past event. The problem is the actual sequence: this passage introduces a restoration problem, describes an ongoing study and then recommends a course of action. It does not organize the evidence as support and counterevidence for a stated hypothesis followed by a revised hypothesis.

Passage A argues that while fingerprint identification may lack uniform scientific standards, it is a valuable and reliable form of evidence that courts should continue to accept. Passage B, in contrast, points out the lack of objective standards and the unknown error rates, challenging the premise that fingerprint identification is as reliable as claimed. *The Most Valuable Sentences:* - Passage A: “this court sees no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time” (P3). - Passage B: “there is no generally agreed-on standard for determining precisely when to declare a match” (P1).

**Passage A: Court Response to the Challenge**

The defendant in a criminal trial challenges the fingerprint evidence used to convict him, focusing on the lack of scientific testing, absence of studies proving the uniqueness of fingerprints, and undefined error rates. He also criticizes the lack of uniform standards among examiners, especially regarding the number of matching features needed for identification.

**P2: Concerns About Standards and Error Rates**

The defendant argues that examiners don’t have consistent guidelines and references courtroom testimony that there's no standard for “points of identification.” He emphasizes that error rates for fingerprint misidentification aren't established.

**P3: Court Defense of Fingerprint Evidence**

Although the court concedes that fingerprint evidence isn’t a “scientific law,” it notes a long history of expert agreement on its reliability and widespread courtroom use. The judge acknowledges that more rigorous standards may be helpful, but sees no cause to reject print evidence entirely due to its track record.

**P4: Clarification of Current Standards and Error Rates**

The court further explains that, despite differences between agencies, fingerprint analysis relies on training, proficiency testing, and peer review, maintaining a solid, “exceedingly low” error rate. Thus, the court found the evidence admissible.

**Passage B: Critique of Fingerprint Identification**

B criticizes fingerprint identification methods, arguing there’s no objective, universally agreed standard for declaring a “match.” Practices differ between agencies; some count matching points while others use holistic methods, with no consensus on required similarity.

**P2: Uncertainty About Uniqueness and Probability**

The passage notes that no one knows the practical odds of matching fingerprints. Since prints collected in investigations are often partial or smudged, there’s no definitive answer about how likely it is to find matches between different people, highlighting a major limitation for evidence evaluation.

**P3: Error Rates and Testing Concerns**

B points out that actual error rates for fingerprint identification are largely unstudied in real-world settings. While some tests show few mistakes, they may not be strict enough, and at least one tough test found a 34% error rate, casting doubt on the method’s reliability.

**Summary Comments**

- The two passages present opposite views on the issue: Passage A defends fingerprint evidence, stressing tradition and expert consensus, while Passage B criticizes it for a lack of scientific rigor, objective standards, and clear error rates. - When confronted with scientific evidence in court, it’s common to see debates like this: one side emphasizes reliability and practicality, the other presses for methodological consistency and proof. - Both passages are helpful examples for questions that ask for the author’s attitude or request you to identify flaws or gaps in the opposing argument’s reasoning.

**Topic**

The slow recognition and eventual discovery of nuclear fission, and why such breakthroughs can be overlooked despite mounting evidence.

**Framework**

Old / New + Theme / Example (The passage uses the story of nuclear fission as a case in point showing how major scientific advances don’t always follow evidence smoothly; it pivots from “old” misconceptions to the crucial new insight.)

**Main Point**

Major scientific advances, such as the discovery of nuclear fission, often lag behind the accumulation of evidence because scientists may overlook or dismiss key possibilities until someone makes the right theoretical connection. *The Most Valuable Sentence appears at the start of the passage:* “Advances in scientific understanding often do not build directly or smoothly in response to the data that are amassed...”

**P1: Introducing the Problem – Scientific Advances Don’t Follow Evidence Smoothly**

The author sets up the idea that scientific understanding does not always progress step by step with the data; sometimes key breakthroughs get missed for years, as shown by the delayed recognition of nuclear fission.

**P2: Prior Theoretical Predictions and Lack of Receptiveness**

Although some theorists had suggested atoms could break apart, the experiments by Fermi’s group weren’t focused on that and researchers weren’t really expecting it. They saw nuclear fission as so unlikely it was like a pebble bringing down a whole house.

**P3: Experimental Evidence Accumulates Amid Expectation Biases**

Experiments by Meitner, Fermi, and others produced confusing results, like odd radioactive byproducts. But these clues went unrecognized due to technical challenges and, more importantly, because everyone expected any products to be similar to uranium—not something as different as barium. Hahn’s eventual discovery of barium as a product seemed to defy what nuclear physics “knew” at the time.

**P4: The Conceptual Link – Meitner’s Insight**

Meitner connected the evidence to the theory and realized nuclear fission had actually occurred. She published her findings, and only then did the scientific community realize all the evidence was already there—they just had been missing the right conceptual framework.

corrections.before:
There were earlier theoretical developments discussed in the beginning of paragraph 2, but the physics community didn't ****neglect**** them, i.e. *fail to consider*.

The physics community ****rejected**** them. They listened to the idea that it was possible to break an atom apart, but they thought the idea that their experiment, involving bombarding uranium with neutrons, would be as likely to involve splitting atoms apart as it would be for a pebble through a window to collapse a house.

There was a ****common view**** that this "theoretical possibility" was, in principle, possible, but it wasn't going to happen in practical reality.

I can see being somewhat tormented by this answer, but it's a stretch to say that the calculations produced by some theoretical physicists qualify as "a theoretical development", and it's a stretch to say that by considering and rejecting this idea, the physics community was ****neglecting**** this deveopment.

corrections.before:
The only calculations discussed come from the theoretical researchers at the beginning of the 2nd paragraph. The physics community seems to accept the legitimacy of the calculations, in principle, but thinks we're never gonna see an atom get split in real life.

They reevaluated that ****interpretation / evaluation**** of the calculations, but they never reevaluated the calculations.

corrections.before:

corrections.before:

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Ousmane Sembène’s unique adaptation of film to West African oral storytelling traditions

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy

**Main Point**

Sembène stands out not just for his sociopolitical commitment, but for successfully fusing Western filmmaking with the forms and techniques of West African oral culture, allowing him to reach a broad local audience and create distinctive films.
The core idea is outlined in the first paragraph: “his originality as a filmmaker lies most strikingly in his having successfully adapted film, originally a Western cultural medium, to the needs, pace, and structures of West African culture.”

**P1: Sembène’s Sociopolitical Commitment and Originality**

Sembène intentionally makes his films about more than entertainment—they’re meant to raise consciousness about society. What really sets him apart, though, is how he adapts Western filmmaking to fit West African oral traditions, making his work accessible to all Senegalese people.

**P2: Elements from West African Storytelling in Sembène’s Characters and Motifs**

His movies pull directly from traditional West African storytelling—using symbols (like trees), stock characters (like the trickster), and predicaments that represent common struggles. Just like oral tales, his characters are more like “types” than individuals.

**P3: Narrative Structure Inspired by Dilemma Tales**

Sembène structures many of his films like West African “dilemma tales,” which are meant to spark debate and interpretation among the audience. His stories often have open-ended conclusions (sometimes literally using freeze-frames) to encourage viewers to actively engage and decide the outcome themselves.

**P4: Initiatory Journeys and Binary Oppositions**

His stories often follow a journey that changes the main character—and hopefully, the viewer, too—mirroring oral tales of personal transformation. He highlights social change through juxtapositions like good vs. evil or powerlessness vs. power, drawing on oral tradition’s use of opposites more than, as some critics assume, Marxist ideas.

This is the sort of correct answer on Inference questions that is just testing technicalities of language. It's not an important idea; it's just a provable idea.

In the middle of the 2nd paragraph, in the sentence beginning with "Also examined --", we're told that the primary source material for analyzing Tucker's acting technique were the ten still available films in which he appeared.

Are ten films a preponderance of the films in which Tucker performed?

First of all, what the F does *preponderance* mean? It basically means "a majority" in this case.

Criminal courts use a standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt" to convict. Civil courts use a standard of "a preponderance of the evidence" to convict. It means that the prosecution has convinced the court that the defendant is more likely than not guilty (more than 50% chance).

So ... how many films did Tucker perform in? In the first paragraph, we were told "he acted (i.e. performed) in 20".

Is 10 most of 20?
No, 11 or higher would be most of 20.

So if this primary evidence for analysis of Tucker's acting were 10 out his 20 films, then the analysis ****is not based**** on a preponderance of his 20 films.

Do you hate this test / your life yet?
corrections.after: Paragraph 1 says Tucker acted in 20 films. Paragraph 2 says the analysis of his acting technique used the ten still available films. Ten out of twenty is exactly half, not a preponderance or majority. Thus the analysis did not closely examine most of the films in which he performed.

The rest of the 2nd paragraph is saying that we tend to think of "simple" (preindustrial) societies as being comprised of happy people. In the case of the !Kung, their lives seem uncomplicated. They seem to have enlightened attitudes about parenting and undeniable charm.

But the end of that paragraph is saying there are harsh, ugly truths within this society. Half of them die before marrying. Many children and siblings perish. There are fights over food. This undermines the idyllic vision we have of children growing up in "simple" circumstances.

*Misconception:* this is a simple, primitive life. Kids grow up without the complications of industrialized societies. It's just Life Classic®, and we're happy they're happy.

*Reality*: this is a harsh, brutal life for kids.

corrections.before:
This is brutally tempting. If it said "empathize" it would be correct.

If I hear about a terrible typhoon in Southeast Asia, and I sympathize with their tragedy, that means that I *feel great sorrow* for their misfortune.

If I hear about a terrible typhoon in Southeast Asia, and I ****empathize**** with their tragedy, that means that I *can totally relate, because I was in Louisiana during Hurricane Katrina.*

Empathy = recognizing similar shared experiences.

That's the concept that we need to get out of this answer choice, in order to support the idea that Nisa's experience ****illuminates**** (shows us) what women's experience in general is like.

I can sympathize with someone, even though their life experience doesn't reflect mine at all.
corrections.after: Sympathizing with someone's suffering does not establish that the person's experiences reveal shared issues across cultures. A respondent may feel sorrow for Nisa without having faced similar dilemmas. D directly supplies common issues among women in a different culture, so it more clearly supports the generalization. Replacing a single word with 'empathize' would not by itself settle that evidentiary comparison.

before.heading: Supporting Text
before.body:
The sentence they point us to seems to partly indicate the contextual reference "potent Western literary convention", because it says,

*****by casting 'Nisa'*** ***in the shape of a "life"******, Shostak employs a potent Western literary convention.*

So does that mean that a potent Western literary convention is "writing stuff in the shape of a life"? It should. But what exactly does *that* mean? Let's hunt for more context.

The sentence we're asked about begins with "Indeed", which means it's continuing a sentiment forward from the previous sentence.

The previous sentence was saying
*Nisa's autobiography is a distinct narrative in a particular voice, but it is manifestly the product of a collaboration*.

Huh? How is that connected, by "Indeed", to the idea that Shostak employs a potent literary convention by casting *Nisa* in the shape of a 'life'?

Let's check the sentence *after* the one they're pointing us to. The author says that *****real***** *lives, in fact, do not easily arrange themselves as stories that have recognizable shapes.*

Okay, it makes a little more sense how this relates to our sentence.

The author is saying *****real***** *lives* as a contrast to the previous sentence's use of 'life' in quotes, and both sentences reference the shape, or lack thereof, of a life. Let's crystallize the comparison:

****Shostak's** ***Nisa*** **vs. In fact****

shape of a "life" real lives, not prone
to recognizable shape

shaped story not easily arranged into
stories, from seemingly
featureless background

The author is basically saying in this last paragraph, that real lives are boring and messy and don't actually have good storylines.

If we had left it up to Nisa to tell her own story, we'd get boring crap like, "We lived in that place, eating things. Then we left and went somewhere else."

But, because Nisa's story is interwoven with the dialogue between Nisa and Shostak, Shostak is able to create a shaped story from this seemingly featureless background.

So by cleaning up Nisa's boring, messy life into a shaped story of a 'life', Shostak is employing a potent Western literary convention.

after.heading: Supporting Text
after.body: The author explains that real lives do not readily arrange themselves into stories with recognizable shapes. Nisa's quoted account gives a sequence of movements and activities without that developed narrative form. Through dialogue between Nisa and Shostak, a shaped life story emerges. The Western literary convention therefore concerns giving lived experience a coherent narrative shape; it does not mean Nisa's life was inherently boring or that her contribution could be discarded.

corrections.before:
We're looking for something like "a shaped story". I'm not sure what "expository comparison" even means.

*Exposition* = background information. When you give a little opening context before the story starts, that's called exposition. An expository comparison would mean a comparison offered for the sake of providing contextual information.

But exposition is information, not narrative. It occurs before we hear a story, or as a pause-button in the story, but it is never the story itself.
corrections.after: The relevant convention is shaping a life into a story. An expository comparison explains by comparing, but no comparison performs the shaping function described here. Exposition need not always occur before a story; that timing rule is not the reason this choice fails.

corrections.before:
We're looking for something like "a shaped story". This is by far our best answer.

Is it weird? Yes, a little. Why are they throwing *novelistic* in there? It's not necessary; they're just trying to make it less clear that this answer is good.

It seems like the passage is talking about *narrative* storytelling:
beginning / middle / end
rising action / climax / falling action

But that is essentially the same as novelistic storytelling, i.e. the type of storytelling we'd commonly find in a novel.
corrections.after: Novelistic storytelling fits the process of shaping lived events into a recognizable narrative. The passage emphasizes how dialogue produces that shape. It does not require any particular sequence of rising action, climax and resolution, nor does it imply that the account is fictional.

before.body:
This quote is one of my favorite LSAT moments. I can't read "We lived there, eating things, then we left and went somewhere else" without chuckling. It's the most boring, vacuous statement ever. Not exactly quote-worthy.

Why did the author bring it up? What does it exemplify? Well it literally says *for example* right before the quote, so the quote must be exemplifying the idea right before the colon.

"Real lives, in fact do not easily arrange themselves as stories that have recognizable shapes".

after.heading: Anticipate
after.body: The words 'for example' connect the quotation to the preceding claim: real lives do not readily arrange themselves as stories with recognizable shapes. Nisa's brief sequence of living, eating and moving illustrates an account without a developed narrative shape. That function, rather than a judgment about the worth of her life, points to B.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The debate over the impact of invasive (nonindigenous) species on ecosystems—are they a dangerous threat to biodiversity, or are their effects mostly misunderstood?

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

There are two competing views: Passage A argues that invasive species are a serious threat to ecosystems and biodiversity, even in rich, undisturbed habitats, whereas Passage B argues that most invasive species simply increase biodiversity or change ecosystems rather than destroy them, and the alarm is often due to human preferences, not ecological collapse.
**The Most Valuable Sentences:** - Passage A: "Now, however, ecologists realize that when humans introduce new species into existing ecosystems, even pristine, species-rich habitats are threatened." (end of P1) - Passage B: "But 50 years of study has failed to identify a clear ecological difference between an ecosystem rich in native species and one chock-full of introduced species." (mid-P2)

**P1 (Passage A): Shift in Scientific Consensus**

Conservationists used to think invasive species were only a problem in disturbed habitats with weak native species, but now they realize even healthy, untouched ecosystems are at risk, and the damage from invasives is a big growing concern.

**P2 (Passage A): Specific Examples and Consequences**

Invasive plants can dramatically alter habitats and reduce native biodiversity, as seen with the Australian melaleuca trees outcompeting saw grass in the Florida Everglades, leading to habitat losses for wildlife, and Scotch broom in Australia wiping out native reptiles.

**P1 (Passage B): Challenging the Threat Narrative**

The real problem with invasive species may be humans' perceptions of nature, since invasions usually add to local biodiversity instead of directly wiping out native species. The change is rarely a strict species-for-species swap.

**P2 (Passage B): Nature Is Transformed, Not Destroyed**

Invasive species don’t cause ecosystems to disappear; they transform them, sometimes making them less appealing to humans, but there’s no evidence that they inherently destroy ecological function the way events like clear-cutting do.

**P3 (Passage B): A More Nuanced Perspective**

While some invasive species cause real harm, most settle in without issue, so the key question is not whether we’ll have “nature,” but what kind of nature we’ll have in the future.

corrections.before:
"Inconsistent" is used pretty consistently on LSAT to mean "self-contradictory".

A's first paragraph didn't say that these ecologists use any self-contradicting criteria for defining an ecosystem.
corrections.after: A does not discuss how ecologists define ecosystems or claim that their criteria vary inconsistently. Differences in definition need not be formal logical contradictions; either way, no such criticism appears here.

corrections.before:
This is clearly a negative sentiment, because Passage B is saying "Y'all are conflating / confusing one thing for another".

To the author of Passage B, whether the Everglades is its original "pristine" sawgrass-bedecked ecosystem or whether its the Everglades 2.0 with Australian trees hovering above, they're both equally ****natural****. In fact, the latter ecosystem has even more biodiversity.

So for Passage A to imply that this updated Everglades ecosystem is *unnatural* is offensive to Passage B. She is saying, "You're just mad because this ecosystem doesn't look the way you wanted it to. It's not as useful or attractive to you. That doesn't mean it's *unnatural*. It's definitely natural, in the physical sense. It's only unnatural to ****you**** in your arbitrary sense of what this ecosystem *should* look like, in the ideal."
corrections.after: B distinguishes physical ecosystems from human ideals about what ecosystems should contain. On that view, an ecosystem transformed by introduced species remains part of nature even if people value it less. Calling it less natural confuses the physical system with a preferred version of it. B says invasions often increase local biodiversity, but does not establish that the particular Everglades invasion increased it.

corrections.before:
The author of B was saying, "an outside species being introduced into a native ecosystem isn't necessarily a bad thing. It just changes it. It's not a disaster."

This answer portrays B's main point as, "the only way a native ecosystem can ever get better is when it absorbs an outside species that's introduced to it".
corrections.after: 'Can only benefit' rules out harmful consequences. B explicitly concedes critical exceptions, including costly damage and tragic extinctions, so that absolute optimism is too strong. The phrase does not mean that borrowing is the only possible way for cultures to improve.

corrections.before:
The particular phenomenon being discussed by both passages is *invasive species*.

Passage A isn't questioning any common assumption about invasive species. It discusses the old view of them before telling us about the new view.

Passage B isn't upholding some common assumption about invasive species. If anything, passage B is debunking the common notion that invasive species are scary / worrisome.
corrections.after: A does question an older assumption about vulnerability, but B does not establish that assumption as well-founded. B's main argument is that introduced species generally transform ecosystems rather than destroy them, while allowing damaging exceptions. That is different from defending Elton's view about which habitats are most vulnerable.

corrections.before:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Can sovereigns (like monarchs or parliaments) truly have unlimited legal power, and what are the consequences of such power?

**Framework**

Answer / Explain

**Main Point**

The passage discusses the paradox of sovereign omnipotence—if a sovereign has unlimited power, it can limit itself, contradicting true omnipotence—and explores how this paradox has practical consequences, such as making it hard for monarchs to make credible commitments (like repaying debts). While constitutional limits (like those after England’s Glorious Revolution) can help, they don’t eliminate the paradox; they just shift it elsewhere in government.
**The Most Valuable Sentence:** Final paragraph: "For example, the constitutional settlement imposed by the Glorious Revolution did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another."

**P1: Introducing the Paradox of Omnipotence**

Can a sovereign really have unlimited power? If so, it should be able to limit itself, which creates a contradiction. This is the paradox of omnipotence.

**P2: Real-World Problems from Sovereign Omnipotence**

This isn’t just a philosophical riddle—it caused real problems for monarchies like those in England and France, who faced big challenges because of it.

**P3: Credibility Problems for Sovereigns**

Sovereigns with unlimited power can break promises whenever they want—especially financial ones—so no one trusts them, and it’s tough for them to borrow money cheaply or easily.

**P4: Historical Example—England and France**

Because kings could always ignore commitments, lenders charged them higher interest rates. Monarchs got a reputation for breaking promises, which made it expensive and challenging to raise money.

**P5: Solution via Constitutional Limits**

The Glorious Revolution changed things in England: Parliament took over the money side of government, represented people with an interest in property rights, and made it so the Crown had to honor its debts—making it easier and cheaper to borrow.

**P6: Limits of Constitutional Limits**

Even though it’s now common wisdom that constitutions help by limiting power, the passage points out that the core paradox remains; now, it’s Parliament that can’t truly limit itself. The problem hasn’t been solved—just shifted.

before.heading: Research
before.body:
In the last paragraph, the author is *Challenging a Position*.

The conventional opinion is that when you have a constitutional arrangement, such as when Parliament was established, you can benefit a sovereign by limiting their power.

And the author is saying that constitutions can fail in this regard.

Fail how?
- doesn't benefit the sovereign?
- doesn't limit the power?

The following sentence clarifies that the constitutional settlement "did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another".

"Omnipotence" is a synonym for power, so the author is saying that having a Parliament did not solve the problem of unlimited power; it just shifted who possesses that unlimited power.

The monarchs used to have sovereignty, and thus lacked the power to restrain its own power. And now Parliament has sovereignty and lacks the power to restrain its own power.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
If we were trying to predict an "If premise, then conclusion" link like we do on LR Principle questions, we'd be looking for something like,

"If sovereign power is just relocated from one entity to another entity, then the paradox of sovereign omnipotence has not been solved.

after.heading: Research
after.body:
In the last paragraph, the author is *Challenging a Position*.

The conventional opinion is that when you have a constitutional arrangement, such as the 1688 settlement that gave Parliament control of Crown finances, you can benefit a sovereign by limiting their power.

And the author is saying that constitutions can fail in this regard.

Fail how?
- doesn't benefit the sovereign?
- doesn't limit the power?

The following sentence clarifies that the constitutional settlement "did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another".

"Omnipotence" means unlimited power, so the author is saying that having a Parliament did not solve the problem of unlimited power; it just shifted who possesses that unlimited power.

The monarchs used to have sovereignty, and thus lacked the power to restrain its own power. And now Parliament has sovereignty and lacks the power to restrain its own power.

after.heading: Anticipate
after.body:

"If sovereign power is just relocated from one entity to another entity, then the paradox of sovereign omnipotence has not been solved.

corrections.before:
The author's "conclusion" is definitely about the adequacy of a solution to a political problem, because she's saying that the constitutional settlement "**did not** solve the paradox of omnipotence", which is a political science problem.

In practical terms, it *did* solve a problem. Whereas the Crown was getting charged terrible interest rates on loans, that went away once Parliament was established.

It did not solve the theoretical issue. Whereas the Crown previously had sovereignty and lacked the power to bind its own power, now Parliament had the exact same situation.

The author would say we should judge whether the problem of sovereign omnipotence was "solved" based on these theoretical considerations. Since they didn't change, the problem wasn't solved.
corrections.after:
The author's "conclusion" is definitely about the adequacy of a solution to a political problem, because she's saying that the constitutional settlement "**did not** solve the paradox of omnipotence", which is a political science problem.

In practical terms, it *did* solve a problem. Whereas the Crown was getting charged terrible interest rates on loans, that went away after the constitutional settlement.

It did not solve the theoretical issue. Whereas the Crown previously had sovereignty and lacked the power to bind its own power, now Parliament had the exact same situation.

The author would say we should judge whether the problem of sovereign omnipotence was "solved" based on these theoretical considerations. Since they didn't change, the problem wasn't solved.

corrections.before:
The *effects* of the problem of unlimited sovereign power were the prohibitively high interest rates that creditors were charging to loan money to the British government.

Once Parliament was established as a check on the Crown's power, the borrowing rates were lowered. So the establishment of Parliament did eliminate the *effects* of the problem of unlimited sovereign power.

But, since it just relocated unlimited power from the Crown to Parliament, it didn't solve the fundamental cause, which is that a sovereign entity lacks the power to bind its own power.
corrections.after: The settlement reduced the Crown's borrowing difficulties by placing its finances under Parliament's control. But the author argues that the underlying inability of a sovereign to bind its own power remained, now in Parliament. Treating that remaining cause as a failure to solve the problem relies on the distinction between removing effects and removing the fundamental cause. The passage describes a change in Parliament's control, not Parliament's creation.

corrections.before:
This principle helps to adjudicate which form of unlimited legal power is *preferable*.

The author doesn't opine on whether having an omnipotent Parliament is an improvement over having an omnipotent monarch.

The author's main sentiment is that the creation of Parliament didn't solve the problem of sovereign omnipotence. The author provides a supporting reason for that view.

The author would probably agree that in practical terms, having unlimited power with Parliament worked out better for England in terms of its lower borrowing rates, but that discussion doesn't take place in the final paragraph, which is what this question stem is asking us about.
corrections.after:

The author doesn't opine on whether having an omnipotent Parliament is an improvement over having an omnipotent monarch.

The author's main sentiment is that the constitutional settlement didn't solve the problem of sovereign omnipotence. The author provides a supporting reason for that view.

The author would probably agree that in practical terms, having unlimited power with Parliament worked out better for England in terms of its lower borrowing rates, but that discussion doesn't take place in the final paragraph, which is what this question stem is asking us about.

corrections.before:
We're looking for "monarchs refused to pay back loans" or "monarchs had to borrow at higher interest rates".

We'd love to hear "it became increasingly harder for monarchs in England and France to borrow money at lower interest rates".

This answer is saying that it **got easier** for regular rich people. We know that regular rich people were more trusted by lenders and offered lower interest rates than were monarchs.

But rich people's interest rates were lower not because their borrowing terms *improved*, but because monarch's borrowing terms got worse.

Perhaps both rich people and monarchs were paying 3% interest rates on loans. But then monarchs earned a reputation for reneging on debts. And not surprisingly, creditors took that behavior into account and demanded higher interest rates from monarchs ("It used to be 3%? Well, not it's gonna be 10%?")

It hasn't become increasingly easy for wealthy subjects to borrow. They're still at 3%.
corrections.after: The passage compares the rates charged to monarchs with those charged to wealthy subjects. It does not describe a trend in wealthy subjects' access to loans. Their comparatively favorable rates need not have improved over time.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
What were we told about *Parliament*?

In the last two paragraphs, we have details like this:
- Parliament controls the Crown's purse strings
- Parliament represents business people that will not tolerate the government walking away from debts or obtaining what they want by force
- Parliament got more favorable borrowing rates because lenders trusted Parliament to pay them back
- Parliament lacks the power to bind itself / it lacks legal power over its own legal power (now *it's* the omnipotent sovereign)

before.heading: Goal
before.body:
None of those have an obvious tie-in to "making a commitment to be a permanent member of an multinational body", so it's hard to make a specific prediction.

But the correct answer will have to lean on something from the "basket of bullet points" we just gathered.

after.body:

- Parliament represents business people that will not tolerate the government walking away from debts or obtaining what they want by force
- The Crown got more favorable borrowing rates because lenders trusted it to honor debts under parliamentary control

But the correct answer will have to lean on something from the "basket of bullet points" we just gathered.

corrections.before: One of the things we know about Parliament is that it ****can**** obtain credit on favorable terms. Why would committing to this multinational body change that?
corrections.after: The passage says the Crown's credit terms improved after Parliament gained control of its finances. It gives no link between the proposed multinational commitment and worsening credit terms. It does not report Parliament's own borrowing terms.

corrections.before:
This reinforces something we already know, without asking us to add something new. We know that Parliament now has sovereign omnipotence. It has the legal authority to do anything it wants. That's what the author meant when he said that creating Parliament "did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another ... Parliament now lacks the power to bind itself".

Before, the Crown had the power to walk away from its commitments, but after 1688 we hear of "the Crown's newfound inability to dishonor its commitments".

Meanwhile, since omnipotence has now just been relocated to Parliament, it is now Parliament that has the ability to dishonor its commitments.
corrections.after:
This reinforces something we already know, without asking us to add something new. We know that Parliament now has sovereign omnipotence. It has the legal authority to do anything it wants. That's what the author meant when he said that the constitutional settlement "did not solve the paradox of omnipotence but just relocated the problem from one branch of government to another ... Parliament now lacks the power to bind itself".

Before, the Crown had the power to walk away from its commitments, but after 1688 we hear of "the Crown's newfound inability to dishonor its commitments".

Meanwhile, since omnipotence has now just been relocated to Parliament, it is now Parliament that has the ability to dishonor its commitments.

corrections.before:
We were told that commercial interests had a more positive feeling about Parliament than they did about the crown.

Why would commercial interests be bothered by this commitment to this multinational body? Maybe they would, maybe they wouldn't, but we don't have any way to support that they would.
corrections.after: Parliament represented commercial interests that would not tolerate governmental disregard for property rights. Nothing tells us how those interests would assess membership in the proposed multinational body.

corrections.before:
The Rio Grande is the area from which corridos came, but they're not a current tourist attraction.

They flourished from 1836 - 1930. Also, brochures tend to provide short snippets about fund touristy activities, not three paragraph essays about musical forms.
corrections.after: The passage explains the history, conventions and social role of a folk-song form. It gives no visitor-oriented information such as where to hear performances or what to visit, so E is a better fit. The historical flourishing dates do not establish that corridos cannot be a present tourist attraction.

corrections.before:
The Rio Grande is the area from which corridos came, but they flourished from 1836 - 1930.

Why would a contemporary newspaper be writing about them?

The other difficulty with this answer is "editorial", which indicates that the author is writing persuasively to argue for an opinion.

Meanwhile, this passage felt dry and informative.
corrections.after: The tone is explanatory rather than an editorial argument about a contemporary issue. A newspaper could discuss historical music, but this passage's organized account of a song form fits E more closely; its historical subject alone does not exclude newspapers.

corrections.before:
The passage was about a musical form, the corrido, not about specific lives.

A couple specific people are mentioned, but we don't know they're famous and don't get any biographic information about them. They are just singers of certain corridos.
corrections.after: Cortez appears as the hero of a song, not as a singer identified by the author. The passage focuses on the corrido form and uses songs as examples; it does not recount the lives of famous regional figures.

corrections.before:
We just read the two sentences we have about the origins of corridos in the Spanish ballad tradition (the 2nd and 3rd sentences of the passage). There was nothing in there about corridos using much of the same imagery.

It says that corridos use ****formal features**** of several different types of folk songs, but it doesn't say they share any ****imagery**** with Spanish ballads.

It's very unlikely that they *would* share much imagery, since the corridos are famous for using local imagery (the 2nd paragraph is the only time we speak of imagery and its all local cowboy in Kansas stuff, which probably didn't show up in too many ballads from Spain).
corrections.after: Spanish roots and shared formal features do not establish shared imagery. The passage describes familiar images in corridos but does not compare them with Spanish ballad imagery. Familiar storms could appear in different traditions, so their local relevance does not prove the proposed overlap unlikely either.

corrections.before:
This is a tough correct answer for most of us, because it's counterintuitive. The author actually singled out the despedida as "perhaps the ****clearest**** marker of the corrido's uniqueness and genre".

It sounded like "hearing the despedida would be a clear giveaway that this is a corrido", so why would the author say that a corrido *without* a despedida would probably still be identifiable?

Well, there are a few moments we can cobble together:
- that last sentence says that the despedida is "perhaps" the clearest marker of the corrido's uniqueness, not definitely. That means the author is thinking, "hmm, maybe there are other markers of corridos' uniqueness that are even clearer than the despedida".

If the author thinks that something else might be the clearest marker of the corrido's uniqueness, then it makes sense that even without a despedida we could probably still tell it's a corrido.

- the first two sentences of the last paragraph talk about ready-made lines that travel from one ballad to another, and then the says that the despedida is where that's *most* evident. But this statement also allows for negative space, where ready-made lines traveling from one corrido to another are still *somewhat evident* elsewhere, outside of the despedida.

- the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph -- "such imagery ... readily ****recognizable**** to corrido listeners"

- the last sentence of the 1st paragraph -- "****heavy**** reliance on ****familiar**** linguistic and thematic ****conventions****."
corrections.after: The despedida is described as perhaps the clearest marker, but the passage also identifies recognizable imagery, ready-made lines and familiar linguistic and thematic conventions. Those other features support probable identification even when the closing verse has not survived. 'Perhaps' softens the ranking; it does not by itself prove that the author thinks another marker is clearer.

corrections.before:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

How plants’ distinctive smells and tastes (from secondary chemical substances) have evolved, especially through interactions with insects.

**Framework**

Old / New and Answer / Explain

**Main Point**

Plants contain unique secondary chemical substances—mainly for attracting or defending against insects—and this chemical arms race has driven the evolutionary specialization between plants and plant-eating insects.
The "most valuable sentence" for the main point is near the end of P2: "Other secondary substances that arose by mutation were conserved by natural selection because they proved to be biochemical defenses against the enemies of plants, the majority of which are insects."

**P1: Basic Plant Chemistry—Primary vs. Secondary Substances**

Plants all have “primary substances” (things like proteins and carbs) they need for survival, but the interesting “secondary substances”—unique to different plants and responsible for their taste and smell—don’t impact their basic function.

**P2: Why Plants Have Secondary Substances—Insects and Natural Selection**

These secondary substances evolved because of genetic mutations, but only stuck around if they provided an evolutionary advantage, mostly by either attracting helpful insects (like pollinators with appealing scents) or defending against harmful ones (with bad tastes, toxins, or warning smells).

**P3: The Ongoing Evolutionary Battle between Plants and Insects**

Plants and insects have been locked in a chemical arms race for ages: as plants develop new defenses, insects are forced to adapt or find new food. Over time, this has led to insect species specializing in eating just a few types of plants—basically, both sides have become more and more choosy!

**P1: Basic Plant Chemistry—Primary vs. Secondary Substances**

Plants all have “primary substances” (things like proteins and carbs) they need for survival, but the interesting “secondary substances”—unique to different plants and responsible for their taste and smell—have no known role in the internal processes of growth or metabolism.

**P2: Why Plants Have Secondary Substances—Insects and Natural Selection**

These secondary substances evolved because of genetic mutations, but only stuck around if they provided an evolutionary advantage, mostly by either attracting helpful insects (like pollinators with appealing scents) or defending against harmful ones (with bad tastes, toxins, or warning smells).

corrections.before:
There's no way we're reaching into future paragraphs to answer a Local Purpose question (once in a blue moon, we might reach into a previous paragraph).

Also, insects have only affected plant evolution when it comes to secondary substances (as far as we know).

So "primary substances" are not a second way that insects have affected plant evolution.
corrections.after: Primary substances provide a contrast that clarifies secondary substances. They are not presented as a second way insects influence plant evolution. Context elsewhere can help explain local purpose, but here it does not supply the proposed two-way distinction.

corrections.before: With primary substances, there **isn't** a great diversity. They're "found in all plants".
corrections.after: The author emphasizes that primary substances are required for growth and functioning and occur in all plants. That contrast helps define the more variable secondary substances. Being found in all plants does not, by itself, prove a category contains little chemical diversity.

corrections.before:
The only "most" fact about plants we get in the passage is the 2nd sentence:

*most plants contain two categories of chemical substances: primary and secondary*

This answer is about "most plants w/ chemical defense systems". We definitely don't have any generalization about that subgroup that would allow us to say what is true of most of them.

In the final paragraph we hear that when a plant develops a chemical defense system, "the insects [that eat that plant] must switch to other foods or evolve ways to circumvent the plants' defenses."

This answer choice is saying **more than 50%** take the 2nd option, but we can quantify that. Maybe most of the time insects just switch to other foods.
corrections.after: The passage does not quantify how many chemically defended plants remain food for a wide variety of insects. It describes insects shifting foods or evolving countermeasures, then emphasizes increasingly restricted food ranges for individual insect species. That does not establish this claim about most plants.

corrections.before:
The passage is suggesting the opposite of this. It's saying (P2) that "Insects appear to have played a major role in many plants' having the secondary substances (like toxic chemicals) they have today."

The passage is saying that secondary substances first appear as random mutations, but the survival advantage conferred by some of these mutations (because of the insects that otherwise eat these plants) made these traits naturally selected for, i.e. this mutation got passed onto subsequent generations because it helped the plant survive.

Nothing in the passage is saying that many of these secondary substances evolved independently in various species. The final paragraph is stressing how "for hundreds of millions of years there has been an evolutionary competition for advantage between plants and plant-eating insects".

The emergence of secondary substances that eventually become a trait of the plant species is dynamically related to the insects that are preying on that plant.
corrections.after: The passage does not report scientists' views about the independent origin of the same toxic substances in unrelated plant species or their survival in only a few species. **Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The conflict between two foundational economic ideas—Adam Smith’s Pin Factory (increasing returns to scale) and Invisible Hand (competition)—and how the struggle to mathematically represent increasing returns shaped economic theory.

**Framework**

Old / New (With elements of Highlight Noteworthy, but primarily Old / New)

**Main Point**

For almost two centuries, economic theory favored the easily modeled idea of diminishing returns (ignoring increasing returns and the Pin Factory) because it was more mathematically manageable, until late 20th-century advances finally brought the concept of increasing returns into mainstream economics. **The Most Valuable Sentence(s):** The last paragraph has the most direct statement of the main point: “Only since the late 1970s has this ‘underground river’—a term used to describe the role of increasing returns in economic thought—surfaced into the mainstream of economic thought. By then, economists had finally found ways to describe the Pin Factory with the rigor needed to make it respectable.”

**P1: Introduction—The Central Contradiction**

Warsh’s book highlights an old contradiction in economic theory going all the way back to Adam Smith: the opposing ideas of the Pin Factory (increasing returns from specialization) vs. the Invisible Hand (the market’s reliance on competition).

**P2: Explaining the Pin Factory and Invisible Hand**

This paragraph dives deeper into Adam Smith’s two famous examples: the Pin Factory (showing how specialization and scale make production more efficient) and the Invisible Hand (showing how personal self-interest leads to public benefit through competition).

**P3: Explaining the Contradiction**

Here, the passage spells out why these two ideas clash: increasing returns favor big firms and lead to monopolies, while the Invisible Hand requires lots of competitors—so they can’t both work together in a free market. Economic theory, therefore, depended on the assumption of diminishing (not increasing) returns.

**P4: The Dominance of Diminishing Returns**

For about 200 years, economists mostly ignored increasing returns, not because they didn’t matter, but because it was easier to do elegant math with diminishing returns. Economics wanted mathematical rigor, and increasing returns just didn’t play nicely with equations.

**P5: The (Re-)Emergence of Increasing Returns**

Even though increasing returns were obviously important in real industries (like railroads), economists struggled to rigorously prove their ideas. It wasn’t until the late 1970s that better mathematical tools allowed increasing returns—the Pin Factory—to finally join the mainstream, ending its time as an “underground river” in economic thought.

Is there any supporting text that shows us how the author feels about Pin Factory?

In the 2nd paragraph, the author seems to present Pin Factory and Invisible Hand as two phenomena that are both real, but are opposed.

The 4th paragraph begins by saying,

*For almost two centuries, the assumption of diminishing returns dominated economic theory, with the Pin Factory de-emphasized. Why?*

The fact that the author is confused here reveals that her expectation is that both concepts, which are both valid, would have prominent roles in economic thinking.

The strongest line reference comes from the beginning of the last paragraph, because that's where we find the keywords "mainstream of economic thought".

corrections.before:
The attempts to mathematically model two competing economic assumptions, Pin Factory and Invisible Hand, resulted in the former being de-emphasized (because they couldn't come up with the math for it) and the latter dominating economic theory for almost two centuries (because they could come up with the math for it).

Can we say that a 200 year domination that results from attempts to model is "describing the tensions"?

It would be kind of like taking a paragraph to describe a football game whose final score was 77 - 3, and then saying that we "described the tensions resulting from watching that game". There was no tension. It was a blowout!

We could try to stretch this language to say, "the resulting tension was a LACK of tension!" but normally when you talk about the tension between two ideas or schools of thought, you're talking about gridlock or competing interest or compromise.

You're not talking about two centuries of the one thing beating the other.
corrections.after: Paragraph 3 explains the tension between increasing returns and the competition needed for the Invisible Hand. Paragraph 4 explains why the more mathematically tractable assumption dominated economic theory. It does not say the conceptual tension resulted from attempts at mathematical modeling. One theory's dominance would not, by itself, prove an absence of intellectual tension.
