This gives us "relaxed standards" and "fewer workers", neither of which match up with our two descriptors of increasing returns. If anything, having each worker specialize on a narrow task sounds like the opposite of *relaxed* standards.

- huge increases in efficiency that are achieved through increased size

- each worker has more specialization on narrow tasks
corrections.after: Productivity improves because standards are relaxed, not because a larger organization permits greater specialization. Specialization and relaxed standards need not be opposites; neither scale nor a scale-driven division of tasks explains this improvement.

corrections.before:
This answer still goes along with the author's suggested relationships:

"increased size -> more increasing returns -> smaller firms who can't keep up with lower costs disappear -> industry becomes dominated by just a few players -> monopoly"

In order for this sort of idea to weaken, it would need to say that once an industry is dominated by only a few players, the other ones can't drive each other out of business, and so it never gets down to being dominated by only one company (a true monopoly).
corrections.after: Collusion by a few dominant firms is compatible with the monopoly power the author is concerned about. It does not weaken the earlier link from increased scale and lower costs to the displacement of smaller firms. corrections.before:
This is tough to like on a first pass, in part because we need to use or remember the sentence *before* the author starts talking about monopoly:

*the bigger the pin factory, the more specialized its workers can be, and thus the more productive (more pins per worker) each worker can be*.

This was the author's basis for the first connection in her causal chain:
"****increased size -> more increasing returns**** -> smaller firms who can't keep up with lower costs disappear -> industry becomes monopolized by just a few players".

This answer is going against that link by saying, "Sure, as you get bigger, you get more specialized, and so you might derive more productivity out of each worker. ****But --**** that doesn't necessarily give your business some comparative advantage over smaller businesses. After all, there are also ****downsides**** to becoming more specialized, such as your workers hate their repetitive, specialized jobs and so they more frequently quit and so you more frequently have to pay to find / interview / hire / train new workers."

This answer doesn't directly speak to monopoly power; it tries to kill that causal chain farther upstream, denying the basic starting point that bigger businesses, due to their greater ability to specialize workers, start to have an important economic advantage over smaller businesses.

This is definitely a "best available" answer situation, where the others don't do anything or go the wrong way, so this one ends up winning by comparison.
corrections.after: The author's chain depends on greater specialization giving large firms a cost advantage that lets them displace smaller competitors. If other costs offset the productivity gains once workers are very specialized, that advantage need not keep increasing with scale. This weakens the chain before monopoly power is reached. The choice specifies training costs and turnover, but does not establish why workers leave their jobs.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The exercise of selective enforcement and legal discretion: when and why authorities choose not to enforce laws or rules literally, illustrated by law enforcement and by a real-world municipal case about overdue water bills.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain (Passage A); Problem / Solution (Passage B); The passages together also illustrate Theme / Example (with B as an example of ideas in A).

**Main Point**

Passage A: Law enforcement agencies frequently use their discretion to not prosecute certain violations because laws are often written too broadly, and enforcing them strictly would be impractical and unfair. The author explains that nonenforcement helps prevent excessive costs without opening up too many loopholes. (Most Valuable Sentence: "But there is a technique—discretionary nonenforcement—by which the costs of overinclusion can be reduced without a corresponding increase in underinclusion (loopholes).")
Passage B: Rather than using typical property-related debt collection methods (liens), city officials plan to cut water service to a select few as an enforcement measure, due to a legal loophole that prevents them from placing liens on water debt. The passage questions whether changing the law would be a better solution.

**P1: Passage A - Introduction to the Power of Nonenforcement**

Law enforcement can effectively ignore certain laws by choosing not to prosecute some violators, and the author sets out to explain why this is common.

**P2: Passage A - Why Laws Are Overinclusive and the Value of Discretion**

Laws are usually written too broadly, catching behavior that lawmakers didn't intend to ban, because it's hard to perfectly capture every scenario. Strict enforcement would be costly and could punish the innocent, but giving enforcement agencies discretion allows them to avoid these issues without making the law full of loopholes.

**P3: Passage A - Limits and Oversight of Discretionary Enforcement**

While enforcement agencies could theoretically use their discretion capriciously, in reality they're kept in check by legislative oversight, so their discretion typically aligns with what lawmakers intended the law to achieve.

**P1: Passage B - The City's Selective Enforcement Plan**

The city has tens of thousands of people behind on their water bills, but instead of going after everyone, officials want to selectively cut service to some high-income residents to make an example and encourage compliance.

**P2: Passage B - Alternative Enforcement Methods**

The author suggests a more standard way to collect the debt—placing liens on properties—would be more effective and fair, as is common practice with other debts.

**P3: Passage B - The Legal Loophole and a Call for Legislative Change**

A legal technicality prevents the city from using liens for water bills (since they're not considered taxes). The passage questions why officials don't just change the law instead of resorting to cutting off water. In summary: Passage A explains the logic behind selective legal enforcement and the dangers of strict literal enforcement. Passage B gives a real-life example of selective enforcement, highlighting the limitations imposed by the law and questioning whether changing the law would be preferable to making harsh examples.

before.heading: Research
before.body:
The needed context to most *Meaning in Context* questions is found just before the actual word / phrase.

When we're asked what a term was referring to, sometimes it could reach even further back into the passage.

So let's start from the beginning of the 3rd paragraph. We had just established that our solution to laws with vague, overly inclusive language is to leave it up to prosecutors to use their discretion in terms of how they apply this law.

We're hoping they will enforce the law when the violation accords with the spirit of why the law was written. We're hoping they will use their discretion and not-enforce the law, when violation seems like an accidental technicality, not the actual intent of the law.

The beginning of the 3rd paragraph acknowledges that when we give this discretionary power to law enforcement, we don't actually give them a rulebook for how they implement this power.

"Conceivably (it's possible, the author acknowledges), that prosecutors might choose to spend their finite resources by going after the harmless people who violate the law in one of those accidental, unintended ways. But this seems unlikely."

The author is saying, "There aren't any rogue prosecutors that are so weird or vindictive that they want to use these overly inclusive laws to go after people who aren't actually the target of these laws."

So *capricious enforcement* is code for this sort of behavior. When someone in authority makes a *capricious* decision, we're saying it's not grounded in reason or substance. It's just done arbitrarily for a personal whim.

before.body: We want something that sounds like, "a law enforcement agency chooses to enforce a law against accidental-violators, not the people actually targeted by the spirit of the law".

Because the homes in the neighborhoods are similar in price, it causes (results in) economic segregation.
​

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Communication among animals—especially the mechanisms, symbolism, and interpretation of honeybee dances, and examples of symbolic animal communication more broadly.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain (both passages focus on explaining how honeybees communicate the location of food sources, while Passage B also situates this in the broader context of animal symbolic communication)

**Main Point**

**Passage A:** The main point is that researchers have uncovered that honeybees communicate the location of food sources to nestmates through dancing that utilizes low-frequency sounds, rather than odors, to convey information. (Best encapsulated in the final sentences: “Finally, using a honeybee robot to simulate the forager’s dance, Kirchner and Michelsen showed that sounds emitted during the forager’s dance do indeed play an essential role in conveying information about the food’s location.”) Passage B: The main point is that some animals, such as bees and vervet monkeys, communicate symbolically (with bees’ dance conveying complex info about food), but animals do not blindly follow symbolic signals—they interpret them in context. (The Most Valuable Sentence is: "He found that hive members ignored the foragers’ instructions, presumably because no pollinating flowers grow in such a place.")

**P1 (Passage A): Early Discoveries about Bee Communication**

Scientists have been fascinated by how bees communicate food locations since ancient Greece, with Aristotle observing dancing bees. Later, in the 1940s, von Frisch cracked the dance code, realizing bees were conveying specific information, but the details of *how* they transmitted this info were still unclear.

**P2 (Passage A): Search for the Physical Mechanism—Sound or Smell?**

The 1960s brought discoveries about the actual signals bees use: researchers noticed bees make low-frequency sounds while dancing. Although initially dismissed (since many believed bees couldn't hear), Wenner suggested odors, not sounds, might be the crucial info source. The debate was unresolved.

**P3 (Passage A): Evidence for the Importance of Sound, Not Odor**

Further research proved bees can direct nestmates to food sources they themselves hadn't visited—impossible if scent was necessary. Experiments with a dancing honeybee robot confirmed that dance-emitted sounds are indeed essential for communicating food locations.

**P1 (Passage B): Symbolic Communication Across Animal Species**

All animals communicate, but some (including bees and vervets) communicate symbolically. In an experiment, vervet monkeys responded to different alarm calls with appropriate reactions, suggesting that their calls symbolically represent different kinds of predators.

**P2 (Passage B): Honeybee Dance as Symbolic Language; Olfactory Debate**

Von Frisch described the bee dance as a form of symbolic language, conveying info about where and how good a food source is. Some researchers thought bees used smell in addition to dance, but that's not supported by evidence.

**P3 (Passage B): Animal Communication Is Not Blindly Followed**

Bees don't just automatically act on all information given — in a clever experiment, bees were told (via dancer) about food in a lake, but the hive ignored the advice since flowers don’t grow on lakes. This shows bees use judgment, not just reflex, when responding to communication.

In an uplift fee contingency agreement, the client and the lawyer aren't subjecting themselves to different levels of financial risk.

Since the lawyer is the one undertaking all the financial risk, according to this payout scheme of "the returns will be divided in proportion to the financial risk assumed", that would mean that the lawyer would get 100% of the payout.

Problem / Solution (with a dash of Present Debate)

corrections.before:
Passage A does talk about how companies are now motivated to stockpile patent portfolios, as a deterrent against patent lawsuits, but it's far from the main point, which is a broader discussion of the Problem with software patents.

Passage B is way off, though. It's reluctance, not an apology. And it's a passage that is seemingly addressed to an audience *internal* to the company, like its board of directors or shareholders or employees. It's not a front-facing press release to customers.

Customers don't need to know that a software company is amassing a patent portfolio to ward off scurrilous lawsuits.
corrections.after: A's discussion is broader than developing a defensive deterrent: it explains the problems with broad and obvious patents. B explains a reluctant defensive policy, rather than apologizing to customers. The passage does not identify its audience as exclusively internal or establish that customers would have no reason to know the policy.

before.body:
The first answer that comes to mind is that both authors would say that software companies would be wise to stockpile their own patents so that they have a credible deterrent protecting them from being sued by others for patent infringement.

That was Passage B's resigned conclusion. That passage was an apology to people internal to the company, "Sorry that we have to join this stupid era of patent hoarding, but we'd be stupid not to protect ourselves".

At the end of Passage A's third paragraph, it says, "a fundamental mistake [software companies often made] is not joining this arms race".

corrections.before:
This aligns with our predictions.

The 3rd paragraph of Passage A talks about companies stockpiling patents as a deterrent to other companies, warning that there will be possible retaliation (countersuits) were they to be sued for patent infringement.

And Passage A says that "a fundamental mistake" is when software companies ****don't**** join this arms race. So we can flip that to derive that passage A would say they would be well-advised ****to**** join this arms race.

Passage B is writing an internal memo to explain why they are deciding to amass their own portfolio of software patents. It's common sense that if they are taking this action, they consider it a well-advised action.
corrections.after: A calls not joining the defensive arms race a fundamental mistake that can leave a company defenseless. B says prudence dictates adopting a patent portfolio for defensive purposes. Those stated evaluations support the shared recommendation, without needing to infer an internal audience or an apology.

corrections.before: Passage A never warns companies, "You better not infringe on anyone's patents". She seems to think a ton of modern patents are for obvious stuff that shouldn't have been granted a patent, so she definitely isn't suggesting that everyone respect and obey the existing patents.
corrections.after: A describes how difficult it is to discover and license all relevant patents; neither passage presents complete avoidance of infringement as its recommended strategy. That does not establish that the authors oppose respecting valid patents. Their supported shared advice is to build defensive portfolios.

corrections.before:
Correct answers on Strengthen and Weaken are almost never as weak as "some / sometimes".

This doesn't give us any way to argue that patents facilitate innovation in software development.
corrections.after: Self-interested motives for opposition do not show whether patents actually impede innovation. The claim concerns the effect of patents, not the purity of opponents' motives. corrections.before:

If everyone were able to steal your invention once you finished it, then it wouldn't be worth putting years of your life into developing it. But ... if you can patent your invention so that you have 20 years of exclusive rights to it, then you have assurance that you can make a bunch of money off your invention, thereby justifying the efforts you invested in creating your invention.

If you couldn't patent software, software innovation would be less profitable, so businesses would be less interested in software innovation, so less software innovation would occur.

Thus we're making the case that patents don't impede innovation, they solidify a strong incentive for innovation.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
The central topic of the passage is the relationship between *Calvaria major* and the dodo bird.

Why was the author writing about this? What framework did we use?

The author is initially explaining the research of Temple, who posited a causal connection between the extinction of the dodo and the struggle for *Calvaria major* to continue surviving.

There are 3 paragraphs of fairly neutral description of Temple's research, so it feels for a while like a *Highlight Noteworthy* type passage, just presenting someone else's ideas. Temple's ideas constitute a sort of *Answer a Question* type passage, since he is trying to solve the causal mystery of why *Calvaria major* trees seem to be disappearing.

But then the 4th paragraph rolls into town and it basically debunks Temple's hypothesis. The author agrees with these skeptics, saying they "strongly challenge" Temple's proposal.

He reacts to Wendy's data by saying, "So *Calvaria major* **in fact** is not struggling like Temple thought". Then he says, "Additional counterevidence comes from Speke, which **shows** that [something else Temple thought was wrong." And the passage finishes by saying the mystery that Temple was trying to solve "could easily be due to other factors".

So we would probably call this a *Present Debate* passage, since we have more than one non-author opinion. The author does seem to clearly take the side of the people in the 4th paragraph.

Thus, let's look for something like, "Temple's theory that *Calvaria major* is dying off because of the extinction of the dodo is not well supported by data and undermined by possible alternative explanations."

CAUSAL CLAIM:
Sally was late because of the accident on the highway.
SUPPORTABLE INFERENCE:

ANTI-CAUSAL CLAIM:
Sally's tardiness had nothing to do with the highway accident.

If an animal like a dodo or turkey digests the seed, it will wear down that wall somewhat (abrade it) and make it more likely that the seed will germinate.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is telling the story of a discovery that broke a long-held rule about what infections look like — and explaining how it works and what it might mean.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author isn't arguing against an opponent; they're showcasing a discovery and tracing its consequences.

**Main Point**

Here's the simpler version: scientists used to think every infectious agent had to carry genetic material — DNA or RNA — because that's how all the known ones reproduce. Then researchers studying CJD found something that breaks that rule: a pathogen made just of protein. They called it a "prion." Prions reproduce by changing the shape of other prions on contact, which is why they cause damage and why the body can't fight them. The discovery opened a whole new category of pathogen and might help explain other brain diseases too.

**P1: The old rule**

To count as a pathogen, an agent has to reproduce inside the host. Every known pathogen reproduced using DNA or RNA, so people assumed all pathogens contain genetic material.

**P2: The exception**

While hunting for the cause of CJD — a degenerative brain disease — scientists isolated something with no nucleic acid, just protein. They called it a prion.

**P3: How prions cause harm**

Prions are normally harmless proteins. But once one folds into the bad shape, it converts the next prion it touches into the same shape, which converts the next, and so on. That chain reaction creates plaques in the brain that kill nerve cells. Two important consequences: the body doesn't see prions as foreign (they're your own protein), and there's no therapy that stops the cascade — so CJD is always fatal.

**P4: Acceptance and a wider implication**

The prion idea was treated with skepticism at first but is now widely accepted. The author closes by noting that misfolded proteins might also play a role in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's — though the details are still being worked out.

corrections.before:
This has the appealing structural feel of Flip the Fact answers, which are commonly correct on Opinion and Inference.

They almost always relate to Cause / Effect ideas from the passage, and feel like, "If the CAUSE weren't happening, then the EFFECT would not be happening".

So when we see this answer, we should ask ourselves, "Does the ability to abnormally shaped prions to reproduce itself **lead** to CJD?"

Sure -- we're told in P2 that CJD involves the brain becoming riddled with tiny holes, as evidence of nerve death.

And we're told in the middle of P3 how abnormally shaped prions reproduce in an unexpected way, starting a chain reaction that flips normal prions into the weird kind, resulting in a plaque that collects in the brain and ultimately destroys nerve cells.

So the passage did connect the ability of abnormal prions to reproduce to CJD. Hence we can support this Flip the Fact counterfactual that "if they couldn't reproduce, they wouldn't cause CJD".

before.body:
The central topic of the passage is *Katherine Dunham*.

Why was the author writing about her? What framework did we use? What would be the *one* sentence the author could say about her, if he could only communicate one thing to us?

We probably used a *Highlight Noteworthy* framework, since this is mainly a glowing, informative article about someone.

So combining *Highlight Noteworthy* + *Katherine Dunham*, our main point should sound like whatever our author was stressing was distinctive, important, or interesting about her.

The first sentence calls her introduction of "dance-isolation" *one of the more **striking** (i.e. Noteworthy) developments in modern American Dance.*

So the main point will probably center around Dunham introducing dance isolation. Why is she or it noteworthy?

The final sentence of the first paragraph sounds like it answers the former: Dunham's success was probably crucially reliant on her training in both anthropological research and choreography.

This idea gets fleshed out in the 2nd paragraph (which affirms that it's an important idea). Dunham was noteworthy for being an one of the first anthropologists to take on dance, and she was uniquely qualified to understand it because she was also trained in dance.

The 4th paragraph mentions that Dunham was distinctive because she got immersed in the dances she was studying (rather than staying detached).

And the 5th paragraph highlights how she then taught these foreign dance styles in America, crucially establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right.

Okay ... like so many Highlight Noteworthy passages, it's hard to limit ourselves to which of these details is most "main point"-worthy.

Let's look for something praising her for introducing dance isolation, and highlighting any of her distinct or noteworthy attributes:
- studied dance when others didn't
- knew how to dance when others didn't
- got immersed in her subject, while others wouldn't
- helped establish African American dance as its own art form

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The relationship between wealth, happiness, and the importance of comparison and perceived success.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain (with a dash of Present Debate on how to interpret rivalry in happiness studies)

**Main Point**

Across both passages, the authors explore why increasing wealth doesn't necessarily make societies happier over time. The key explanation is that people adjust their expectations and compare themselves to others—either due to habituation, rivalry, or a desire to feel successful. (The Most Valuable Sentence is in Passage A, P1: “Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income.” and in Passage B, P2: “Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.”)

**P1 (A): Introduction of the Wealth-Happiness Paradox**

We learn that richer people in a society tend to be happier than poorer people, but as societies get wealthier, they don't necessarily get happier overall. This is because as incomes rise, so do people’s expectations (income "norms"), due to getting used to new standards (habituation) and comparing themselves to others (rivalry).

**P2 (A): How Habituation Works**

Raising living standards feels great at first, but soon people get used to it, so it no longer makes a difference; people's definition of "enough" money moves up as their income does. Job satisfaction is more about increases in pay than about absolute pay.

**P3 (A): Overvaluing Material Goods**

People fail to realize how quickly they adjust to new material possessions, so they end up overemphasizing stuff and sacrificing leisure, thinking those material gains will make them happier than they actually will.

**P4-P7 (A): The Role of Rivalry and Relative Position**

A study (Solnick & Hemenway) shows people prefer a scenario where they earn less overall if it means being ahead of others. Happiness depends on how people stack up to their peers (reference group) rather than on absolute income; for example, East Germans became less happy when they started comparing themselves to richer West Germans.

**P1 (B): Questioning the Interpretation of Rivalry**

The author asks if the desire to be better than others is all about primal competition (one-upmanship), perhaps evolved for mating advantages— but questions whether this evolutionary argument is actually correct.

**P2 (B): Rejecting the Primal Rivalry Theory**

Although the evolutionary explanation is popular, the author points out that evidence doesn’t fully support it. Instead, data suggest people are happier when relative prosperity makes them feel successful and valuable, not just "better" than others.

**P3 (B): It’s About Success, Not Money**

Money itself isn't the source of happiness—it's the sense of being successful and having created value. Even if people have different incomes, if they both feel successful, they’ll have the same happiness.

**P4 (B): Reframing Rivalry as Positive**

The author argues that striving for more isn’t just petty competitiveness—it’s often a desire to create value, which actually benefits society and makes people happier.

The author wouldn't characterize the evidence as "ambiguous" if she thinks *her explanation* is "best supported by the evidence".

If evidence were ambiguous, you wouldn't be able to tell which interpretation is best supported. She actually says, "Rather, the data *show* that" (not a more tentative verb like *might suggest* that).
corrections.after: Passage B does not describe the study as largely ambiguous evidence for a plausible rivalry account. It rejects that account in favor of the claim that relative prosperity makes people feel successful and productive. Evidence can sometimes be ambiguous yet favor one explanation, so the rejection should rest on this author's actual characterization, not a general rule about ambiguity.

corrections.after: Passage A does not explain the phenomenon through biological origins. Passage B presents a primeval mating explanation only to reject it in favor of perceived success and value creation. Presenting an explanation is different from using it to support one's own position.

**Topic**

Why great perfume isn’t considered a serious art form—despite strong similarities to painting and music.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

"Stealing thunder" — the courtroom strategy of revealing a client's damaging information first — and the psychological reasons why it works (with limits).

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author surveys evidence and psychological explanations for why the strategy works.

**Main Point**

Stealing thunder is corroborated as an effective strategy by simulated trials and supported by several psychological mechanisms (credibility, critical assessment, scarcity, framing) — though it has limits when information is very damaging.

**P1: What stealing thunder is**

A lawyer reveals negative client information before opposing counsel can. Pointless if the weakness is unknown or won't be exploited; otherwise, voluntary revelation is less damaging than hostile revelation.

**P2: Why it works — research and three psychological explanations**

No empirical research has tested the strategy in actual trials. But simulated-trial studies suggest it's effective within a reasonable range of applications. Lawyers' belief in the strategy is corroborated by experimental findings and supported by psychological explanations.
(1) *Credibility*: people who reveal information against their own interest are perceived as more credible (a finding from psychological research).
(2) *Critical assessment*: warning juries about upcoming attempts at persuasion makes them resist (in psychological experiments, audiences warned about persuasion become more resistant).
(3) *Scarcity*: a piece of evidence becomes "old news" once the prosecution and defense have both raised it; persuasive messages, like commodities, are valued more when scarcer.

**P3: A fourth explanation — and a limitation**

Stealing thunder works because the lawyer can frame the evidence in his/her own terms and downplay it (like political "spin"). But this works only when the information can be framed positively. Jurors initially have little information and want to solidify their position; they use the early positive framing to guide subsequent analysis. The strategy's limit: when information is very damaging, stealing thunder may create an early *negative* impression that becomes a cognitive framework jurors use to filter subsequent information.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is explaining a courtroom trick called "stealing thunder" — where you tell the jury about your client's weakness *before* the other side does — and why it works.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy.

**Main Point**

The simpler version: when there's bad info about your client that's going to come out anyway, get it out yourself first. Studies of mock trials show this strategy works, and psychology gives several reasons. You look more credible. The jury becomes alert and starts pushing back against the other side's pitch. The damaging info becomes "old news." And you get to put your spin on it. The catch: if the info is really bad, getting it out first can backfire — it sets the wrong frame for everything that follows.

**P1: The strategy**

If your client has a weakness the other side will probably exploit, volunteer it first. That softens the blow.

**P2: Why it works**

Real trials haven't been studied, but mock trials confirm the strategy. Psychology adds reasons: (1) you look credible because you're hurting your own case; (2) warned juries push back harder against the other side; (3) the same evidence from both sides becomes "old news" and loses force.

**P3: One more reason — and the catch**

You also get to spin the bad info on your own terms. Jurors solidify their position quickly, so your early framing sticks. But there's a limit: if the info is really damaging, going first creates an early negative impression that becomes the lens for everything else. So the strategy can backfire.

But the correct answer is saying, "Both passage A and Kant were right -- they can agree we wouldn't lie to a pathological liar since a pathological liar's lies aren't the products of rational decision making."

Absence of a duty does not by itself explain why that first-paragraph rationale supplies no sufficient reason in this case. B directly addresses the relevant condition by denying rationality to pathological behavior.

**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The myth that old window glass flows downward over time, and the science debunking it.

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

The commonly held belief that window glass flows downward over time (causing old windows to be thicker at the bottom) is a myth; scientific calculations and historical glassmaking techniques explain the thickness differences instead. (The main point is most directly addressed at the beginning of paragraph 2 and fully explained in the last paragraph.)

**P1: Introduction to the Glass Flow Myth**

A lot of people (even in science books) mistakenly believe that window glass is a super slow-moving liquid and gradually flows downward, explaining the thicker bottoms in old windows. This myth likely started because glass's atoms are not arranged like in crystals, but the structure alone doesn't mean glass is liquid—it's solid at room temperature, just with a unique atomic arrangement.

**P2: Scientific Debunking**

A recent study shows that, although glass *can* flow under gravity, it would take longer than the age of the universe for old windows to change thickness from flow. So, that's not the reason old windows are thicker at the bottom!

**P3: Why Flow Still Isn’t the Answer**

Even the easiest-flowing glass (like germanium oxide glass) would still take trillions of years to change shape noticeably, and medieval glass—even with impurities—wouldn't flow in just a few centuries. The science is clear: for glass to flow, it actually needs to be heated to at least 350°C.

**P4: Real Explanation—Old Glassmaking Techniques**

Those thicker, rippled old windows are because of how glass was made before modern methods—not because of flow. Old glass was blown, spun, and flattened, which left thicker edges, and it made sense to install panes with the thick part at the bottom. Later techniques produced more even panes, and today’s glass is super-flat thanks to floating it on molten tin.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
The first time the *atomic structure of glass* is mentioned in the passage is in the middle of the 1st paragraph:

*the atoms in glass are not arranged in a fixed crystal structure / the structure of liquid glass and solid glass are very similar, but thermodynamically they're different.*

It then tells us one of the most confusing sentences I've ever read in RC. This sentence / this question sort of live in infamy in terms of difficulty to process the intended meaning.

A freezing point is when a substance turns from liquid to solid. When we're told that "glass doesn't have a precise freezing point", we're saying there's not a specific temperature at which glass turns from liquid to solid.

By contrast, water turns from liquid to solid at 0 degree Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit).

Over the course of ****a few hundred degrees Celsius (!)****, glass *transitions* from liquid glass to solid glass? That's apparently the notion of the glass transition "temperature".

It's an oxymoron to say "the transition temperature is typically a range of a few hundred degrees". By saying *the* temperature, you're indicating that there is an actual number, like 0 degrees Celsius.

But this term is apparently a willful self-contradiction.

In the final sentence of the 1st paragraph, when it says *cooled below the lower end of this range*, we think, "When the temperature is now lower than that 300 degree range where glass slowly makes it way from liquid to solid".

So that means this last sentence is talking about what's true of solid glass, not liquid glass, and yet it says "molten (liquid) glass retains an amorphous atomic structure, but it takes on the physical properties of a solid".

The confusion here comes from the fact that the modifier "cooled below the lower end" implies an action that was applied to liquid (molten) glass.

Put into plainer English, that last sentence says, "When you take liquid glass and cool it all the way down (all 300 degrees or so) until it's fully transitioned to solid glass, it retains the same atomic structure, but it takes on the physical properties of a solid."

This is a callback to the idea that "the structure of liquid and solid glass are very similar, but thermodynamically they are not the same".

before.heading: Goal
before.body: Look for something like, "the atomic structure of glass is such that .... *it doesn't change very much when you go from liquid to solid*?"

after.heading: Anticipate
after.body: Paragraph 1 distinguishes atomic arrangement from physical behavior. Glass retains an amorphous atomic structure as it cools through a transition range, yet below that range it has the physical properties of a solid. The passage uses transition temperature for a range, not a precise freezing point. Paragraphs 2 and 3 add that solid glass can flow slightly, while appreciable flow requires substantial heating. Keep the distinctions between atomic structure, temperature range and noticeable flow separate.

after.heading: Goal
after.body: Test each claim against those distinctions. Heating can change flow behavior without requiring a fixed crystalline arrangement.

corrections.before:
This is saying that glass always behaves as a solid.

If say, "My dog begs for food even when there's food in his bowl", we mean that he *always* begs for food, whether there's food or not food.

So this answer is saying that whether glass has gone full liquid or full solid, it will behave as a solid.

The end of the first paragraph was making it sound like molten (liquid, flowy) glass switches into having the properties of a solid, once you've dipped below its glass transition temperature. But we're not hearing that liquid glass behaves as a solid.

*p.s.* something that makes this answer so frustrating to interpret is the notion of "reaching" your glass transition temperature. Again, that's a self-contradictory notion, because the glass transition isn't a specific value you can reach. It's a range of a few hundred degrees.
corrections.after: The passage guarantees solid physical properties below the lower end of the transition range. It does not guarantee the same behavior after glass has been heated to that range. The phrase even when does not, by itself, mean always under every condition; the problem is the unsupported extension of solid behavior.

corrections.before:
This is an unreasonably hard correct answer to get. It goes counter to the author's main Challenge Misconception purpose, so it's not at all tempting. And it has nothing to do with the end of the first paragraph, where the keywords take us.

But our ultimate measuring stick for "*suggests / most likely to agree / most reasonably inferred*" is just which answer is most supportable.

If you heat solid glass until it becomes liquid glass, do you think it would flow downward under its own weight?

Of course! All liquids would flow downward under their own weight. They're liquids. The force of gravity pulls them crashing to the floor. The concept of *weight* is basically (mass + gravity).

What this answer is trying to do is a common trait of correct answers on Most Supported tasks: they take something that was said one way and present the inverse version of that same thing.

If we learned that, *studying multiple languages reduced people's risk of Alzheimer's*, a correct answer might give that back as *being monolingual has at least some drawbacks to one's health*.

Since we learned that, *cooled* *****below***** *its transition temperature, molten glass takes on the properties of a* *****soli****d*****

this answer is testing us on, *heated* *****to***** *its transition temperature, solid glass takes on the properties of a* *****liquid*****

We could also support this answer from the last sentence of the 3rd paragraph, where it implies that there *is* a way for glass to have a non-negligible rate of downward flow: *it would have to be heated to at least 350 degree Celsius*.

One property of a liquid is that you would flow downward, like a waterfall, or a mountain river. The game on this question for LSAC seemed to be to draw our eyes to the confusing end of the 1st paragraph, present some *wrong* ideas about what that was saying, and then bury this simple idea of "liquid flows downward" in weird language that kind of sounds like the opposite of the main point.
corrections.after: The passage presents glass as retaining an amorphous structure while its physical properties change across the transition range. Together with the account of gravity-induced flow and the need for substantial heating for non-negligible flow, this supports downward flow when glass is heated to its transition range. Do not treat this as a general rule that every conditional can be reversed.

corrections.before:
The author never presents a harsh, conditional relationship that says

"if the atoms aren't fixed crystalline structure, then glass will never stop flowing".

Also, the language of this answer is somewhat nonsensical. By saying, "Glass will stop flowing only if the atoms are arranged in a fixed crystal structure", we'd seemingly be implying that *there is some possibility* that glass's atoms will be in fixed crystal structure.

But we don't think glass will ****ever**** be arranged in a fixed structure, so it would be weird to say the passage suggests this meaning.
corrections.after: Paragraph 1 says glass can take on solid physical properties while remaining amorphous. A fixed crystalline arrangement is therefore not established as necessary for solid behavior. The answer adds an unsupported only-if requirement.

corrections.before:
There's nothing in our Support Window relating to medieval times or different methods of making glass.

The passage has explicitly told us that the author thinks people belief glass flows downward because they misunderstand the fact that atoms in solid glass are now arranged in a fixed crystal structure.

The answer has to address that provided detail. Any answers pulling wording from other parts of the passage are just trying to tempt us with familiar sounding words.
corrections.after: The proposed source of confusion is a misunderstanding of glass's noncrystalline atomic structure, not an assumption that medieval and modern manufacturing methods were similar.

corrections.before:
There are two implied comparisons between medieval glass and modern glass:

1. medieval glass is thicker at the bottom than modern glass is

2. medieval glass contains more impurities than modern glass does

Could either of those comparisons translate into a higher glass transition temperature?

A higher glass transition temperature would mean that if you cooled liquid glass (medieval and modern), the medieval glass would start taking on the physical properties of a solid sooner, because it transitions at a higher temperature.

We know that the author doesn't think that #1 is related to glass transition temperature, because she explains in the final paragraph that it's more related to manufacturing methods.

When it comes to impurities, all we know is that impurities in medieval glass would make the warmer, more liquid-y version more prone to flowing downward (the impurities "lower the viscosity and speed the flow").

The medieval glass is more prone to being liquid-y, whereas higher glass transition temperature would mean that it becomes a solid sooner than modern glass does (which makes the modern glass sound more liquid-y).

So, if anything, this answer seems to go against the passage. But rather than getting too lost in that deep technical rationale, we can feel fine eliminating this based on not having any good way to compare glass transition between medieval and modern.
corrections.after: The passage describes impurities in medieval glass and differences in manufacturing methods, but gives no comparison of medieval and modern transition temperatures. Neither the relative amount of impurities nor its effect on transition temperature is established here.

corrections.before:
This answer is combining two facts:
- glass takes a few hundred degrees to go from solid to liquid (it doesn't flow like a liquid until it's closer to the upper end of those few hundred degrees)

- glass doesn't start acting like a liquid at all until you're at at least 350º

Thus, we can tell that at 350º, with only a negligible ability to flow, glass has NOT yet completed the journey through its glass transition temperature. It still has a ways to go, and thus the upper end of the glass transition is well above 350º.

This is a brutal correct answer, and it requires that we do some searching in the passage, because 350º isn't anywhere near our Support Window at the end of the 1st paragraph.

We have to ask ourselves agnostically, "Hmm ... did we say anything about 350 degrees?"

The end of the 3rd paragraph says:
*for glass to have more than a negligible ability to flow, it would have to be heated to at least 350 degrees Celsius*.

Remember that glass transition temperature is defined as the range of a few hundred degrees over which glass goes from solid to liquid, or liquid to solid (depending on whether you're heating a solid into a liquid or cooling a liquid into a solid).

Let's say for Glass X, its glass transition range is from 25º - 325º Celsius. That would mean that at any temperature below 25º, glass is acting like a solid. At any temperature above 325º, it's acting like a liquid. Any temperature in between, like 150º, would be a hybrid. It would be a "very viscous liquid" or a "somewhat spongy solid".

Could there be a glass like Glass X, which is totally liquid by the time it hits the upper end of its glass transition temperature at 325º?

No. That would contradict the line we just read that, "glass doesn't really flow at all until you get above 350º". By the time Glass X gets to 325º, it has fully transitioned into a liquid form, so it would flow like water or like maple syrup. It sounds more like a typical transition temperature would be that Glass X goes from solid to liquid as we go from 300 - 600º Celsius. That would be more in line with the idea that as you get to around 350º, the glass starts to be able to flow downward somewhat (because it's loosening from solid form to liquid form).
corrections.after: Combine the transition range of a few hundred degrees in paragraph 1 with the statement in paragraph 3 that more than negligible flow requires heating to at least 350 degrees Celsius. In that account, 350 is a lower threshold for appreciable flow, rather than the upper end of the transition range. This supports an upper extreme well above it. The passage does not supply exact endpoints such as 300-600 degrees, and none should be invented.

Why do we think that the author opened with a quote by Kotzebue, from 1806, about Beethoven, given that the main focus of the passage was about Schoenberg?

The author is definitely tracking some sort of analogy or similarity, because directly after the quote, she says:

*This remark* *****aptly characterizes***** *the reaction of many listeners to Schoenberg.*

Okay, author, but then why aren't you just quoting someone who actually listened to Schoenberg? Why are you bothering to compare him to Beethoven?

The 3rd paragraph starts to clue us in to the intended comparison between B and S.

Many listeners reacted to both of their music with harsh criticism and dislike. Both of them *stirred controversy* because of the way they altered the language and extended the expressive range of music. (Hmmm, that sounds positive)

The rest of the 3rd paragraph is reminding us that nowadays Beethoven is universally cherished as one of the best composers ever.

Is the author's purpose to suggest that Schoenberg will also one day come to be appreciated?

Yes, we ultimately discover, but we really don't know how positive an impression the author has until we get to the final paragraph.

Since the author clearly appreciates Schoenberg (he makes essential music that captures emotional states never before recorded, and he unflinchingly faces difficult truths), the author seems to build the Beethoven comparison throughout the passage in order to show the parallels of provocative geniuses who were resisted in their time but who people eventually realized were geniuses.

before.heading: Anticipate
before.body:
This is a Local Purpose question (in order to / serves to / primarily to), so we're trying to think about the Bigger Idea that's happening in this immediate vicinity.

We know that the function of this last paragraph is for the author to challenge the position of people all worried about the negative impact of biotech patents.

Our author starts with a concession, "it's true, worried people ... it *used* to be the case that we freely shared research materials (the opposite of tightly controlled patented discoveries) and now we've shifted to a market model (which highly incentivizes using patents protectively)".

We know the rhetorical logic of this sentence "While it is true that X, it is also undoubtedly true that Y" means that the 2nd half has to have the opposite purpose from the first half.

Since the first half of the sentence was trying to acknowledge the merits of the worried people, the second half of the sentence should be trying to downplay the legitimacy of the worried people.

"Yes, even though there's a bigger market emphasis now, ... *y'all shouldn't be so worried about the influence of biotech patents on basic research,* *****because***** *...* even in the early days of biotech, researchers would take measures to prevent competitors from gaining access to materials they had innovated."

In other words, the protective secrecy that patents give to companies/researchers isn't that different from the measures that researchers have always taken to guard or hide some of their discoveries.

So the author is mentioning "the old days" to downplay the worries of the people in the 2nd paragraph, indicating that what's currently going on with using patents to hide discoveries is not that functionally different from what this biotech field has historically been used to.

"Patents", the author is arguing, are really just a new means to a classic end.

after.heading: Anticipate
after.body: The first sentence of the final paragraph concedes a shift from communal sharing to a market model, then notes that some early researchers also prevented access to materials. That supplies a precedent for present competitive behavior. It does not show that the frequency or severity of restrictions stayed the same, or that patents and physical access control are identical. Indeed, the next sentences distinguish patent rights from control of access.

corrections.before:
When we're asked for the meaning or function of something in context, there's usually a trap answer that tries to bait people in with the dictionary connotations of a word.

"early days" = "history / evolution"

But the author does not furnish a brief account of the evolution of biotech. The author makes a momentary comparison to the past to say, "There's really not that much more protective secrecy nowadays than there was in the early days of biotech."
corrections.after: The reference to earlier restrictions supplies a specific counterpoint to the current concern. It does not provide an account of the field's overall evolution, nor quantify whether secrecy is more or less common now.

corrections.before:
The author's first sentence is saying, "Yes, we've shifted away from communal sharing and more towards a market model, ****but****, there's really not that much more protective secrecy nowadays than there was in the early days of biotech."

Even then, people would take measures to prevent access to stuff they had created. That's all patents are doing. Same same, but different.

This ain't nothin' new = this is not entirely unprecedented
(i.e. "there's at least some precedent for this")
corrections.after: Some early researchers prevented competitors from accessing materials they created. Present competitive practices therefore have at least some precedent. This limited claim does not equate patent rights with access control or assert that the amount of secrecy is unchanged.

corrections.before:
This answer is such a complicated sentence that we should be suspicious that it's correct. The correct answers on *What's Implied* questions like Opinion and Inference are often aloof, abstract, tortured.

Let's try to break apart the multiple claims:

1. the ancient associations of colors with spirits were important **precursors** to later wampum representations

How do we feel about this? Did the author think the stuff in paragraph 2 was an important precursor to the stuff in paragraph 3?

2. the ancient associations of colors with spirits were important **foundations** to later wampum representations

corrections.before:
The author isn't this far in favor of Steele that she'd be ready to say, "Okay, I'm basically convinced. Some acquired traits *probably do* get passed from one generation to the next".

The last couple paragraphs are saying, "We know that mutated RNA can reverse transcribe back into modified DNA (so experience does have the power to change your DNA), but we're not sure if that modified DNA can actually make it into the reproductive cells and thus be passed on. Steele thinks a virus can do it, but biologists are not convinced by that yet."
corrections.after: The author presents a possible mechanism and disputed circumstantial evidence, not a conclusion that acquired traits probably pass to offspring. Reverse transcription has been observed in other contexts, but its operation in the immune-cell mechanism is itself presented as Steele's hypothesis. That distinction must remain unresolved.

corrections.before:
This is supported by the first two sentences of the 3rd paragraph:

*Steele hypothesizes that the altered RNA then reverts back into DNA.*

If Steele and colleagues had actually observed this reverse transcription, then there would be no need to use the verb 'hypothesizes', which sort of means 'guesses'.

*Indeed, such "reverse transcription" of RNA back into DNA has been observed frequently in other contexts.*

What are these *other contexts* where reverse transcription has been observed? They must be *other than in the context of the immune system*, since the immune system is what we were talking about throughout paragraph 2.

The combination of "we've seen this elsewhere" with "Steele *hypothesizes* that this is going on in the immune system" suggests that Steele has not directly observed this happening in immune cells.
corrections.after: The text says Steele hypothesizes that altered immune-cell RNA reverts to DNA, then contrasts this with reverse transcription observed in other contexts. corrections.before:

Steele is looking at subsets of DNA and seeing stuff within the genetic code that appears to be altered .. there's a *signature*, a cluster of *distinct mutations* that apparently stick out from the rest of those immune response genes.

Similarly, this answer involves looking at the potentially altered text itself and finding within that some stuff that sticks out like a sore thumb: *signature* vocabulary that doesn't seem like part of the original code.

This answer implies that what we're seeing in the surviving text is something typical of the later era but not typical of the original era. It's not super clear how that part of this answer matches Steele and colleagues, but presumably if they are able to pinpoint "a distinct pattern of mutations", then they must have a *control group* idea of what the DNA should look like if it were following the original form.

Mutations are anomalies, and so it presupposes that you know what "normal" is in order for you to detect "abnormal".
corrections.after: Steele points to an internal signature in the present genetic material as evidence of past transfer. Vocabulary characteristic of a later era inside the surviving play likewise serves as an internal trace of later alteration. before.body:
The correct answer to Local Purpose usually sounds like a paraphrase of the Framing Idea that comes *before* the detail(s) we're asked about.

When we find the quote from the UN Charter, and then rewind a sentence or two, do we see any broader claims that this could be unpacking?

Yes! The first sentence is saying that the UDHR "was the **first** international treaty to do X".

The second sentence is saying, "Prior to the UDHR, **no** truly international standard existed".

And then the 3rd sentence begins with "Although the UN Charter in 1945 did Y ..."

This suggests that the author might be qualifying that previous claim with some concession like, "Sure, sure --- in 1945, the UN Charter did something *kinda* like what the UDHR finally did for realsies, but it didn't really do X, or it wasn't a truly international standard for X."

The UDHR was the first to "affirm universal respect for human rights", but the UN Charter 3 years earlier *was* written with the purpose of obligating the UN to "*encourage respect for human rights*".

The second half of the 3rd sentence needs to be telling us how the UN Charter falls short of doing what the UDHR was the first to do, and sure enough the backend of that sentence is saying that people thought that the UN Charter's attempt to safeguard respect for human rights "was not strong enough / didn't go far enough in its efforts to guarantee basic human rights".

They proposed "fixing" the Charter's attempt at guaranteeing basic human rights by creating an obligation for member states to act on it, but the final sentence tells us that "ultimately this proposal and others like it weren't adopted; instead the UDHR was commissioned and drafted".

before.heading: Goal
before.body: The net effect of these quotes is basically like someone saying, "Sure, the UDHR wasn't the first **attempt** to safeguard human rights from the UN, but the previous attempt (the UN Charter) didn't have enough teeth behind it and so people still felt unsatisfied, which motivated the creation of the UDHR."

after.heading: Research
after.body: The question compares two quotations: Article 1 of the UN Charter and the rejected proposal to strengthen it. The Charter obligates the UN to encourage respect for rights. The proposal would require member states to take separate and joint action and cooperate in promotion of rights. The surrounding text explicitly says the group found the original language insufficient and sought to strengthen it.

after.heading: Goal
after.body: Look for comparison of the force of the Charter language with the stronger proposed obligation for member states. The proposal was not the UDHR itself.

corrections.before:
Comparing "the strength of language" can be matched up with a lot of the text from the 1st paragraph. We anticipated something like, "the author tells us about the UN Charter to explain that there **had** been a previous attempt to safeguard human rights, but it didn't have enough teeth behind it, so that's what motivated the creation of the UDHR".

The UDHR "expressly affirms universal respect for human rights", while the UN Charter "*encourages* respect for human rights".

UN members weren't happy with the Charter because they said "the language was not strong enough / it didn't go far enough to guarantee rights".

They "lobbied vigorously to **strengthen** the human rights provisions" and proposed that member states be **required / obligated** to act on human rights issues.

It still seems weird to say that the author's purpose in quoting the Charter and quoting the Proposal was to compare strength of language in each, but the author is telling the backstory that led up to the UDHR, and the crux of that backstory is "Are we being forceful enough in guaranteeing human rights"?

There's a progression from the Charter's weak-sauce "we encourage respect" to the Proposal's obligatory "member states are required to co-operate with the promotion of human rights" to the eventual language of the UDHR.
corrections.after: The first quotation concerns encouraging respect for rights; the second would require member states to act and cooperate. The direct quotations let the reader compare the strength of those formulations. This is a comparison of the Charter and the proposal, not a direct quotation of the later UDHR.

The author then describes a widespread view that conscious intention is uniquely human and uses Maritain’s account of the bee’s dance as an example of that view. The passage does not separately attribute the uniquely-human claim to Grice.

**P3: Passage B - Critiquing the Conventional View**

Here's the pivot: the author says this way of thinking is circular—we define animal communication as non-intentional from the start and then use that as proof. Plus, new evidence (especially from chimpanzee studies) is blurring the lines, making it less clear that human language is uniquely intentional and animals just react automatically.

corrections.before:
This captures the negative vibe. We can support "they make assumptions" from the line that "these arguments are circular: conscious intention ****is ruled out a priori****".

"a priori" is a Latin term (I guess) that means, roughly, prior to even entering this conversation / examining this data.

It comes from the old Nature vs. Nurture debate. How much of our minds is programmed by innate things (a priori) and how much is acquired through experience (a posteriori).

So that first sentence of B's last paragraph is saying, "They begin with an assumption that animals *don't* have conscious intention and then conclude from that absence that animal communication is very different from human communication".

The "should be determined empirically" is somewhat just the logical opposite of *a priori*, but it is also reinforced by the fact that B brings up what *recent research* has told us.

In short, B is like, "Shut up psg A. You're just assuming animals don't have intention, but check the research instead of your ego-reinforcing assumptions. The empirical research suggests there's not this huge gap in communcation."
corrections.after: Passage B objects that conscious intention is ruled out a priori, then its supposed absence is used to distinguish animal communication. In context, the objection is to deciding the issue in advance instead of testing it through evidence. The final sentence cites recent research narrowing the gap, which supports empirical investigation. A priori does not simply mean an innate trait in a nature-versus-nurture debate.

corrections.before:
Psg B never accused thinkers like Psg A of believing that *all* communication systems can be explained in evolutionary benefits.

Also, psg B would probably agree with this (assuming that they're both scientists who believe in the theory of evolution), so she wouldn't say that psg A *falsely* believes that communication can be explained via natural selection.
corrections.after: Passage B does not attribute a claim about all communication systems' evolutionary benefits to the opposing researchers. Acceptance of evolution would not by itself establish that every communication system is explained entirely by adaptive benefit. The dispute here concerns conscious intention and assumptions about it.

corrections.before: No Support Passage B: chimps
corrections.after: No Established Disagreement

corrections.before:
We'd be stretching our guess at what Passage B would say by citing her opinion on chimpanzees, given that she never discussed them.

Our guess is that the author of Passage B would say "sure, they may possess conscious intention / the ability to attribute mental states".

But the author of Passage A could actually agree here, as he singled out chimpanzees as a possible nonhuman exception that could still perceive mental states.
corrections.after: Passage B explicitly mentions recent research with chimpanzees and other animals. Passage A also allows chimpanzees as a possible exception to its general claim about attributing mental states. Their disagreement is therefore not clearly about whether chimpanzees may have that capacity; the broader qualitative-versus-quantitative difference is the supported divide.

corrections.before:
****Central Topic / Purpose****

African American historians / *Highlight Noteworthy*
in 1870 - 1930 or *Answer a Question*

****Main Point****

Instead of the national perspective that mainstream historians had, Black historians were **distinctive** for having a **transnational** perspective. **Why?** For several reasons ... (felt estranged from U.S. citizenship and were instead writing the history for a nation of black people who originated from Africa but were now dispersed across the globe in many nations).

****Passage Map****

P1 - establishes the contrast between mainstream US historians (nationalist perspective) and black U.S. historians (transnational perspective).

P2 - discusses the fuzzy citizenship status of Black Americans and how that created a large emigrationist sentiment.

P3 - discusses the imperialist nationalism of mainstream US historians and how that made Black historians leery.

P4 - provides the author's takeaways, that the Black historians were doing their own sort of nationalism, but rather than writing the history of a nation, they were writing the history of a "nation of people", black people who came from a glorious African past and now were scattered across the globe.

****Other Commentary****

The first sentence presents as a possible thesis for two reasons:
- Many passages that Clarify a Misconception or Highlight Something Noteworthy begin with language like "in contrast to the mainstream / to the typical / to the usually assumed / to what most ___'s have done or studied"
- The second sentence immediately starts to unpack the first.

So we would encode, presumptively, that the Main Point is "Black historians of this era were noteworthy for having a transnational, rather than national perspective".

The second paragraph begins "First, ...", which alerts us to the fact that we are getting the first of the *several reasons* foreshadowed in the second sentence of the passage. Seeing again that we are fleshing out reasons for the first sentence of the passage would solidify our suspicion that the first sentence was the thesis.

Curiously, the author never uses a "Second, furthermore, moreover" to advance her list of several reasons. Instead, the 2nd and 3rd paragraph combine to give us a sense of the reasons why Black historians of the time had a transnational perspective.

The last paragraph moves on from listing reasons and begins the author's evaluation, signified by the classic ****Author's Pivot**** (but / yet / however / recently) that so frequently introduces the Author's voice or main point.

The word 'diaspora' was not one I knew when first reading this, but from context and outside knowledge, it's basically referring to the people and culture of "Post-African" black people around the world. They don't have a sovereign territory or official language, but these black historians felt as though this group of people still constitutes a "nationality" in some sense.

Basically, even if force and circumstance had inserted these people into different nations around the world, the common homeland of their ancestry made them a community (a diasporic community seems to be a physically discontinuous community ... a local high school basketball team's fans form a 'traditional' community, whereas LA Lakers' fans form a 'diasporic' community, because Lakers fans are spread out around the world).
corrections.after:
